title: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
options: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
body.explanation: The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All the other intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve.
option_notes: The recurrent nerve supplies all other intrinsic muscles.
That branch is sensory.
The external branch supplies the cricothyroid.
IX does not supply it.

title: Which structure divides the temporomandibular joint into two synovial cavities?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure divides the temporomandibular joint into two synovial cavities?
body.explanation: The TMJ has an articular disc, so the bones never touch. The joint surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Lateral geniculate body: the thalamic relay for vision.
option_notes: Pineal gland is the small midline gland above the superior colliculi; secretes melatonin.
Thalamus is the large paired grey mass of the diencephalon, the sensory relay.
The thalamic relay for vision.
Mammillary bodies is the pair of round swellings behind the infundibulum (hypothalamus).

title: What do the maculae of the utricle and saccule detect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What do the maculae of the utricle and saccule detect?
body.explanation: The maculae are responsible for static balance, carried by the vestibular nerve with the kinetic signals from the cristae.
option_notes: Kinetic balance is the cristae.
Maculae sense head position and linear acceleration.
Sound is the organ of Corti.
Not pressure.

title: Which gland of the diencephalon secretes melatonin in response to darkness?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gland of the diencephalon secretes melatonin in response to darkness?
body.explanation: Pinealocytes of the pineal gland secrete melatonin in response to darkness, regulating circadian rhythms.
option_notes: The pineal gland secretes melatonin.
The pituitary is controlled by the hypothalamus and secretes other hormones.
The thyroid is in the neck.
The adrenals are on the kidneys.

title: What proportion of corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What proportion of corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla?
body.explanation: About 90 percent decussate as the lateral corticospinal tract to supply the limbs; the anterior tract stays ipsilateral and crosses later at cervical and upper thoracic levels for the trunk.

title: Which nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle?
body.explanation: At the junction of pons, medulla and cerebellum, the flocculus, choroid plexus and emerging CN VII and VIII surround the foramen of Luschka.
option_notes: VII and VIII at the cerebellopontine angle.
Midbrain.
Behind the olive.
Pons.

title: Which nerves emerge behind the olive?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves emerge behind the olive?
body.explanation: Behind the olive: IX, X and the cranial part of XI. XII emerges between the pyramid and olive.
option_notes: IX behind the olive.
X behind the olive.
XII in front of the olive.
VI at the pontomedullary junction.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the optic tract. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What are the stated functions of the paranasal sinuses?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the stated functions of the paranasal sinuses?
options: Warming the blood and filtering it
Producing mucus for the whole airway
Supporting the eyeball in the orbit
body.explanation: The lecture gives two: they make the skull lighter and add resonance to the voice. Infection causes sinusitis.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the frontal sinus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
options: Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere
body.explanation: Anterior lobe of the cerebellum: the smaller part of the cerebellar hemisphere in front of the primary fissure.
option_notes: The smaller part of the cerebellar hemisphere in front of the primary fissure.
Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere is the large part of the cerebellar hemisphere behind the primary fissure.
Cerebellar tonsil is the rounded part of the inferior hemisphere beside the vermis, above the foramen magnum.
Vermis is the midline part of the cerebellum joining the two hemispheres.

title: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
body.explanation: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal, each leaving through the intervertebral foramen at its level.

title: How thick is the cerebral cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How thick is the cerebral cortex?
body.explanation: The cortex covers the hemispheres, 3 to 4 mm thick, with about 10 billion neuron bodies.
option_notes: Too thin.
Too thick.
Too thick.
About 3 to 4 mm.

title: Cutting one optic nerve completely produces which defect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Cutting one optic nerve completely produces which defect?
options: Loss of the nasal field of that eye only
Loss of vision on the right side of both eyes
Loss of the temporal fields of both eyes
Total loss of vision in that eye
body.explanation: Damage at site 1 in the lecture: the entire optic nerve is cut and there is a total loss of vision from that eye.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Thyroid cartilage: the large shield-shaped cartilage with the laryngeal prominence.
option_notes: Cricoid cartilage is the only complete cartilage ring, below the thyroid cartilage.
Arytenoid cartilages is the paired pyramids on the back of the cricoid where the vocal ligaments attach.
The large shield-shaped cartilage with the laryngeal prominence.
Thyroid gland is the butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the trachea, two lobes joined by an isthmus.

title: Which nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the inner surface of the ramus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve enters the mandibular foramen on the inner surface of the ramus?
body.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (from V3) enters the mandibular foramen and runs in the mandibular canal. Its mental branch later exits through the mental foramen.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the internal capsule (posterior limb). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: About how much CSF does the choroid plexus produce each day?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: About how much CSF does the choroid plexus produce each day?
body.explanation: About 500 mL of CSF is produced each day, although only about 150 mL is present at any time; it is renewed several times a day.
option_notes: About 500 mL per day.
Far too little.
That is the volume present at one time.
Too much.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the inferior concha. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: How long is the bony cochlear tube?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How long is the bony cochlear tube?
body.explanation: The cochlea looks like a snail shell: a bony tube 30 mm long and 1 to 2 mm in diameter, spiralling around the modiolus.
option_notes: Too short.
The bony cochlear tube is about 30 mm long.
Too long.
Far too short.

title: The internal jugular vein starts as the continuation of which structure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The internal jugular vein starts as the continuation of which structure?
body.explanation: The internal jugular vein continues from the sigmoid sinus and leaves the skull through the jugular foramen. It ends by joining the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

title: What forms the optic nerve?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the optic nerve?
body.explanation: Photoreceptors convert light; bipolar, ganglion and horizontal cells process it; ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.

title: Which artery is the main supply of the pharynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery is the main supply of the pharynx?
options: The lingual artery of the tongue
body.explanation: The ascending pharyngeal artery, the second branch of the external carotid, is the main supply. The ascending palatine and tonsillar arteries (facial), the greater palatine and pharyngeal arteries (maxillary) and the lingual artery also contribute.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Cerebral aqueduct. Narrow channel through the midbrain, no choroid plexus; a common site of obstruction.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.
Not at the arrow; this is the CSF-filled space around the brain and cord.
Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.

title: Which fraction of the pinna is fixed to the skull?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which fraction of the pinna is fixed to the skull?
body.explanation: The pinna is joined to the skull by its anterior third; the posterior two thirds constitute its mobile part.
option_notes: The back of the pinna is free.
The upper part is free.
Only the front third is attached to the skull.
Most of the pinna is free.

title: From which part of the neural tube does the spinal cord develop?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: From which part of the neural tube does the spinal cord develop?
body.explanation: The caudal end of the neural tube develops to form the spinal cord.
option_notes: The caudal neural tube becomes the cord.
The cranial end becomes the brain.
The crest gives ganglia, not the cord.
The notochord gives the nucleus pulposus.

title: What are the two parts of the inferior constrictor?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the two parts of the inferior constrictor?
body.explanation: The inferior constrictor has a thyropharyngeus part, from the oblique line on the thyroid lamina, and a cricopharyngeus part, from the cricoid cartilage. Cricopharyngeus is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

title: With an orbital floor fracture, what may prolapse into the maxillary sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: With an orbital floor fracture, what may prolapse into the maxillary sinus?
body.explanation: With orbital floor fractures, prolapse of orbital fat into the maxillary sinus may be seen, sometimes accompanied by inferior rectus muscle prolapse.

title: Through which opening does the aqueous fluid pass from the posterior to the anterior chamber?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Through which opening does the aqueous fluid pass from the posterior to the anterior chamber?
body.explanation: Aqueous is formed by the ciliary body and secreted into the posterior chamber. It traverses the pupil to enter the anterior chamber and exits through one of two drainage pathways.

title: What happens to the pupils in darkness?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What happens to the pupils in darkness?
body.explanation: In darkness the reflex becomes inhibited, which results in dilation of the pupil in both eyes.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the frontal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What do the posterior horns receive?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What do the posterior horns receive?
body.explanation: Dorsal horns receive sensory input from afferent fibres entering via the dorsal roots; ventral horns contain motor neurons.
option_notes: Anterior horn.
Lateral horn.
They receive sensory fibres.
CSF is in the canal.

title: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Cuneate fasciculus: the lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.
option_notes: Lateral spinothalamic tract is pain and temperature, in the lateral funiculus.
Lateral corticospinal tract is the main crossed motor tract, in the lateral funiculus.
Gracile fasciculus is the medial part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the lower body.
The lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.

title: What is the obex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the obex?
options: The peak of the fourth ventricle
body.explanation: The obex is the most caudal tip; the fastigium is the peak inside the cerebellum. CSF leaves by the median foramen of Magendie and two lateral foramina of Luschka.
option_notes: The lowest point of the fourth ventricle.
That is the fastigium.
That is Magendie.
Not a nucleus.

title: Which nerve innervates the maxillary sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve innervates the maxillary sinus?
body.explanation: It is innervated by the infraorbital and alveolar branches of the maxillary nerve (V2), receives blood through branches from the infraorbital and superior alveolar branches of the maxillary arteries, and drains its lymph to the submandibular nodes.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the thoracic nerves (t1 to t12). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which veins drain the thyroid gland?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which veins drain the thyroid gland?
body.explanation: Three groups: the superior thyroid vein to the internal jugular (often via the Farabeuf trunk), the middle thyroid veins directly to the internal jugular, and the inferior thyroid veins to the left brachiocephalic vein.
option_notes: Drains into the internal jugular.
Drains into the internal jugular.
These drain the eye.
This drains the face.

title: Which features describe rod cells? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which features describe rod cells? (choose all)
options: They contain rhodopsin, bleached by light
They are used in low light, as at dusk
They are densely packed in the central fovea
body.explanation: Rods are thin and elongated, in two portions. Their flattened disks contain the pigment visual purple, or rhodopsin, bleached by light to initiate the visual stimulus. They are used at low light levels. The central fovea is populated exclusively by cones, which handle colour vision.

title: A patient understands speech normally but cannot produce fluent speech. Which area is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A patient understands speech normally but cannot produce fluent speech. Which area is damaged?
options: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
body.explanation: Broca's area, in the frontal lobe, controls speaking and writing. Wernicke's area handles understanding.
option_notes: Broca's area produces speech.
Wernicke's damage impairs understanding.
The occipital lobe is for vision.
The postcentral gyrus is for touch and pain.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the palatine tonsil. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Why does the adult cord stop short of the vertebral canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why does the adult cord stop short of the vertebral canal?
body.explanation: The cord finishes growing at about 4 years, the vertebral column at 14 to 18, so the cord occupies only the upper two thirds of the canal.
option_notes: It does not shrink.
Not the reason.
A result, not the cause.
The vertebral column grows faster than the cord.

title: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Lateral spinothalamic tract: pain and temperature, in the lateral funiculus.
option_notes: Gracile fasciculus is the medial part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the lower body.
Pain and temperature, in the lateral funiculus.
Posterior spinocerebellar tract is unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum, at the edge of the lateral funiculus.
Cuneate fasciculus is the lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
options: Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Betz cells)
body.explanation: The arrow points to the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, betz cells). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which are sympathetic effects? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are sympathetic effects? (choose all)
body.explanation: Sympathetic: faster heart, mydriasis, bronchodilation, reduced gut activity, sweating, skin and gut vasoconstriction, glucose release. Gut motility and bladder contraction are parasympathetic.

title: According to the lecture, the first order neuron of the visual pathway is which cell?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: According to the lecture, the first order neuron of the visual pathway is which cell?
body.explanation: In the lecture's scheme: first order, cone and rod photoreceptors; second order, bipolar cells leading to the ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve; third order, the neuron from the lateral geniculate body to the visual cortex.
option_notes: Wrong (in the lecture's scheme): the bipolar cell is the second order neuron.
Wrong: ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve; not first order.
Wrong: the lateral geniculate neuron projects to the cortex (third order in the lecture).
Correct: the lecture names the cone and rod photoreceptors as first order.

title: Name the three regions of the hypothalamus.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the three regions of the hypothalamus.
body.explanation: The hypothalamus is divided into supraoptic, tuberal and mammillary regions.
option_notes: Not the classic division.
These are epithalamus parts.
Not the classic division.
Supraoptic, tuberal and mammillary regions.

title: Which structure connects the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure connects the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle?
body.explanation: The interventricular foramina of Monro.
option_notes: Joins third and fourth ventricles.
The interventricular foramen of Monro.
A lateral exit of the fourth ventricle.
The median exit of the fourth ventricle.

title: Which artery supplies the labyrinth?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery supplies the labyrinth?
body.explanation: The labyrinthine artery arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery or directly from the basilar trunk.
option_notes: It supplies the dura.
The labyrinthine artery (from AICA or basilar) supplies it.
It supplies the middle ear and mastoid.
It supplies the auricle.

title: Where does the pineal gland sit?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the pineal gland sit?
options: On the floor of the third ventricle
body.explanation: A small piriform projection from the back wall of the third ventricle, below the splenium, in the groove between the two superior colliculi.
option_notes: That holds the pituitary.
That is the hypothalamus.
Not there.
It sits between the superior colliculi.

title: Which part of the lateral ventricle is the longest and largest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the lateral ventricle is the longest and largest?
body.explanation: It ends at the amygdala.
option_notes: Shorter.
Not the largest in this lecture.
The temporal horn is described as longest and largest.
Variable and smaller.

title: What is the denticulate ligament?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the denticulate ligament?
options: The fibrous anchor to the coccyx
A pial septum to the dura
A thickening of the dura at L1
A ligament of the vertebral bodies
body.explanation: The pia sends lateral connective septa, the denticulate ligament, which insert between the roots and attach to the dural sheath.
option_notes: That is the filum terminale.
Pia extending tooth-like to the dura on each side.
Not this.
Not this.

title: Where does the hypoglossal nerve emerge?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the hypoglossal nerve emerge?
body.explanation: CN XII emerges from the sulcus between pyramid and olive. CN IX, X and the cranial part of XI emerge from the sulcus behind the olive.
option_notes: IX to XI.
VI to VIII.
III.
Between the pyramid and the olive.

title: What is the primary action of the superior rectus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the primary action of the superior rectus?
body.explanation: Superior rectus: elevation, intorsion, adduction. Inferior rectus: depression, extorsion, adduction. Both take the oculomotor nerve.

title: Which of these is part of the extrapyramidal system?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which of these is part of the extrapyramidal system?
options: The posterior limb of the capsule
body.explanation: The extrapyramidal system includes the basal ganglia, the cerebellum and various brainstem nuclei, modulating involuntary movement, balance and posture.

title: Which glands are modified apocrine sweat glands in the eyelid?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which glands are modified apocrine sweat glands in the eyelid?
body.explanation: The ciliary glands of Moll are modified apocrine sweat glands. The glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands at the base of the eyelash follicles.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Posterior (dorsal) horn: grey matter receiving sensory fibres.
option_notes: Cuneate fasciculus is the lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.
Anterior (ventral) horn is grey matter with the motor neurons.
Lateral spinothalamic tract is pain and temperature, in the lateral funiculus.
Grey matter receiving sensory fibres.

title: Which are functions of the aqueous fluid? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are functions of the aqueous fluid? (choose all)
options: Delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing waste
Transmitting nerve impulses to the brain
Producing the oil layer of the tear film
body.explanation: Its functions are delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing waste products, inflammatory products and other cellular debris from the posterior cornea and crystalline lens; providing a low refractive index transparent medium between the lens and cornea; and maintaining intraocular pressure for the optimal shape and alignment of ocular structures.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Vestibule and semicircular canals: the balance part of the bony labyrinth: the central vestibule and the three looped canals.
option_notes: The balance part of the bony labyrinth: the central vestibule and the three looped canals.
Incus is the middle ossicle, between malleus and stapes.
Stapes is the smallest ossicle, its footplate in the oval window.
Malleus is the outer ossicle, its handle attached to the eardrum.

title: How is the adult CSF volume of about 150 mL distributed?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How is the adult CSF volume of about 150 mL distributed?
options: About 125 mL in the subarachnoid spaces and 25 mL in the ventricles
About 25 mL in the subarachnoid spaces and 125 mL in the ventricles
Equally between ventricles and subarachnoid spaces
body.explanation: 125 mL is in the subarachnoid spaces and 25 mL in the ventricles.
option_notes: Most CSF is outside the ventricles.
Reversed.
Not equal.
Most is outside the ventricles.

title: Where does lymph from the tip of the tongue drain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does lymph from the tip of the tongue drain?
options: To the submandibular nodes on one side only
body.explanation: Tip: submental nodes bilaterally and then deep cervical nodes. Anterior two thirds: submandibular nodes unilaterally, then deep cervical nodes. Posterior third: deep cervical nodes, mainly the jugulodigastric.

title: Which cells are found in the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cells are found in the molecular layer of the cerebellar cortex?
body.explanation: The molecular layer contains inhibitory stellate and basket cells and many dendrites.
option_notes: Molecular layer interneurons.
They form their own middle layer.
These are in the granular layer.
Not in the cerebellum.

title: Which glial cells act as the immune cells of the CNS?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which glial cells act as the immune cells of the CNS?
body.explanation: Microglia act as immune cells and remove debris by phagocytosis.
option_notes: Immune cells of the CNS.
Astrocytes support and form part of the blood-brain barrier.
They make CNS myelin.
They support neurons in PNS ganglia.

title: What does the anterior pole of the thalamus form?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the anterior pole of the thalamus form?
options: The floor of the third ventricle
The roof of the lateral ventricle
Back wall of foramen of Monro
body.explanation: The anterior pole forms the posterior wall of the interventricular foramen of Monro, where five veins join to form the internal cerebral vein.
option_notes: The hypothalamus forms the floor.
Not this.
It forms the back wall of the interventricular foramen.
Not this.

title: What closes the oval window?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What closes the oval window?
body.explanation: The lateral wall of the vestibule communicates with the middle ear by the fenestra vestibuli, closed by the footplate of the stapes and the annular ligament.
option_notes: That closes the round window.
The stapes footplate sits in the oval window.
The tectorial membrane is in the organ of Corti.
The basilar membrane is in the cochlea.

title: A patient has a stroke in the left precentral gyrus. Which deficit is expected?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A patient has a stroke in the left precentral gyrus. Which deficit is expected?
options: Weakness of the right side of the body
Weakness of the left side of the body
Loss of vision in both eyes
Loss of hearing in the left ear
body.explanation: The precentral gyrus is the motor strip. Its pyramidal fibres cross in the medulla, so a left-sided lesion weakens the right side.
option_notes: The motor fibres cross in the medulla, so the opposite side is weak.
The same side is spared; the fibres cross.
Vision is the occipital lobe.
Hearing is the temporal lobe, and each ear projects to both sides.

title: What is the piriform fossa, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the piriform fossa, and why does it matter?
options: The opening of the auditory tube
The space above the vocal folds
A fold of mucosa over the epiglottis
A recess beside the laryngeal inlet
body.explanation: The piriform fossa is a deep recess, broad above and narrow below, in the anterior part of the lateral wall of the laryngopharynx on each side of the laryngeal inlet, produced by the bulging of the larynx. Swallowed foreign bodies may lodge there.

title: Where does maximum refraction occur?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does maximum refraction occur?
body.explanation: The lens is transparent and biconvex, enclosed in a capsule suspended by zonular fibres, but maximum refraction occurs through the cornea.

title: Communicating hydrocephalus is caused by:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Communicating hydrocephalus is caused by:
options: Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct by a tumour
Inadequate absorption or overproduction of CSF
Stenosis of one interventricular foramen of Monro
Blockage of the median aperture of Magendie
body.explanation: The pathway between ventricles stays open.
option_notes: That is non-communicating.
Poor absorption or too much production.
Non-communicating.
Non-communicating.

title: What is the uncus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the uncus?
options: The top of the corpus callosum
body.explanation: The fifth temporal gyrus, the most internal, is the hippocampal convolution; its anterior end curves into a hook, the uncus.
option_notes: Not the uncus.
The hooked front end of the parahippocampal gyrus.
Not insular.
Not the fornix.

title: The tapetum separates the temporal and occipital horns from:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The tapetum separates the temporal and occipital horns from:
body.explanation: It forms their lateral wall.
option_notes: Not this.
The tapetum lies between the horns and the optic radiations.
Not this.
Not this.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Foramina of Monro. The interventricular foramina joining each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the paired C-shaped cavities in the hemispheres.
Not at the arrow; this is the cavity between the brainstem and cerebellum.
This is at the arrow: the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.

title: Which muscle is known as the frowning muscle and draws the eyebrows medially and downward?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle is known as the frowning muscle and draws the eyebrows medially and downward?
body.explanation: The corrugator supercilii arises from the medial end of the superciliary arch and inserts into the skin of the medial half of the eyebrow, making vertical wrinkles above the nose.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the parietal lobe. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the gyrus in front of the central sulcus.
This is at the arrow: the lobe behind the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus.
Not at the arrow; this is the deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
Not at the arrow; this is the lobe at the back of the hemisphere.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the anterior triangle. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Superior sagittal sinus. Dural venous sinus receiving CSF; the sinuses drain into the internal jugular veins.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the outlets of the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.
This is at the arrow: the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.
Not at the arrow; this is the cavity between the brainstem and cerebellum.
Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the medulla oblongata. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the nerve at the pontomedullary junction near the midline.
Not at the arrow; this is the large nerve from the side of the pons.
This is at the arrow: the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the cord.
Not at the arrow; this is the top of the brainstem, below the diencephalon.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the tarsal plate. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What does the lateral reticulospinal tract do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the lateral reticulospinal tract do?
body.explanation: The medial tract, from the pons, facilitates movement and increases tone; the lateral tract, from the medulla, inhibits movement and reduces tone.

title: What is the orbital septum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the orbital septum?
options: A layer of smooth muscle that raises the eyelid from the tarsus
A fibrous membrane connecting the tarsi to the orbital margins
The mucous membrane lining the eyelid
A fold of conjunctiva at the medial angle
body.explanation: The orbital septum is part of the tarsal plate. It connects the tarsi to the margins of the orbit, bounds the orbital fat anteriorly and helps limit the spread of infection between the face and the orbit.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Epiglottis: the leaf-shaped cartilage behind the tongue base.
option_notes: Arytenoid cartilages is the paired pyramids on the back of the cricoid where the vocal ligaments attach.
Trachea is the tube of C-shaped cartilage rings below the cricoid.
Thyroid cartilage is the large shield-shaped cartilage with the laryngeal prominence.
The leaf-shaped cartilage behind the tongue base.

title: Which are parts of the epithalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are parts of the epithalamus?
body.explanation: The epithalamus includes the stria medullaris, posterior commissure, habenular nuclei, pineal body and paraventricular nuclei.
option_notes: Part of the epithalamus.
Part of the epithalamus.
Part of the epithalamus.
The mammillary bodies are hypothalamic.

title: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Optic nerve (II): runs from the eye to the optic chiasm.
option_notes: Abducens nerve (VI) is leaves at the pontomedullary junction, near the midline.
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is leaves the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.
Runs from the eye to the optic chiasm.
Vagus nerve (X) is leaves the medulla behind the olive, below IX.

title: A newborn has an open defect over the lower back with exposed nervous tissue and leg weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A newborn has an open defect over the lower back with exposed nervous tissue and leg weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
body.explanation: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of the caudal neural tube.
option_notes: Caudal neural tube closure failure.
Anencephaly is cranial and not survivable.
Hydrocephalus is ventricular enlargement.
Not a neural tube defect.

title: Which structures pass through the optic canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures pass through the optic canal?
body.explanation: The optic canal (in the lesser wing of the sphenoid) carries the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery. The ophthalmic artery does not use the superior orbital fissure.

title: Which cells of the retina generate action potentials?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cells of the retina generate action potentials?
body.explanation: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells produce graded potentials rather than action potentials. Ganglion cells generate action potentials, and their axons join together to form the optic nerve.

title: Which are actions of thyroid hormones?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are actions of thyroid hormones?
body.explanation: Thyroid hormones accelerate enzymatic metabolism (increasing oxygen consumption and heat production), accelerate carbohydrate metabolism (lowering blood sugar), accelerate lipid catabolism, accelerate diuresis, have a hypercalcemic action by accelerating bone resorption, and act on cartilage ossification and growth.
option_notes: They speed up metabolism.
They speed up fat breakdown.
That is calcitonin.
They increase diuresis.

title: Which duct connects the cochlear duct to the saccule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which duct connects the cochlear duct to the saccule?
body.explanation: The basal turn of the cochlear duct connects to the saccule by the ductus reuniens. The saccule and utricle are joined by a Y-shaped utriculo-saccular duct, which expands into the endolymphatic duct and sac.
option_notes: It joins utricle and saccule.
It goes to the endolymphatic sac.
The ductus reuniens joins cochlear duct and saccule.
The crus commune joins two canals.

title: Where does the palpebral conjunctiva become the bulbar conjunctiva?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the palpebral conjunctiva become the bulbar conjunctiva?
options: At the lacrimal punctum, in the lid
body.explanation: The palpebral conjunctiva lines the eyelid and reflects at the superior and inferior conjunctival fornices onto the eyeball as the bulbar conjunctiva, enclosing the conjunctival sac.

title: What shape does the thyroid gland resemble from the front?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What shape does the thyroid gland resemble from the front?
body.explanation: Two vertical lateral lobes joined by a horizontal transverse isthmus. In anterior view the whole looks roughly like an H, or a butterfly, moulded on the aerodigestive axis.
option_notes: The signet ring describes the cricoid.
Two lobes joined by an isthmus look like an H or a butterfly.
That describes one lobe.
Not its shape.

title: Why does a stroke spare the upper face?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why does a stroke spare the upper face?
options: It is supplied by CN V
It lies outside the facial nucleus
body.explanation: The upper face receives bilateral upper motor neuron input; the lower face only contralateral input. So a supranuclear lesion weakens only the lower face.

title: Which is an example of grey matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is an example of grey matter?
options: Outer layer of the spinal cord
body.explanation: Grey matter examples: cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus, the cord's butterfly-shaped centre.
option_notes: The cortex is grey matter.
White matter.
White matter.
White matter.

title: What forms the roof of the maxillary sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the roof of the maxillary sinus?
options: The lateral wall of the nose
The zygomatic process of the maxilla
body.explanation: The maxillary sinus is pyramidal: roof, the inferior orbital margin; floor, the alveolus of the maxilla; base, the lateral wall of the nose; apex, the zygomatic process of the maxilla.

title: Which is the smallest branch of the external carotid artery?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the smallest branch of the external carotid artery?
body.explanation: The ascending pharyngeal artery is the smallest branch, arising posteriorly near the origin of the external carotid, and ascends to the base of the skull between the pharynx and the internal carotid.

title: What is the cauda equina?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the cauda equina?
options: The tip of the spinal cord
A fibrous anchor to the coccyx
body.explanation: The lumbar, sacral and coccygeal roots run obliquely below the conus medullaris, resembling a horse's tail, in the lumbar cistern.
option_notes: The lumbosacral roots below the cord end.
That is the conus medullaris.
That is the filum terminale.
That is the dural sac.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
options: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
body.explanation: Lateral occipital gyri: the gyri on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, at the back of the hemisphere.
option_notes: The gyri on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, at the back of the hemisphere.
Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus is the middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus, part of Broca's area.
Cuneus is the wedge of medial occipital cortex between the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci.
Insula is the cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Arachnoid granulations. Arachnoid projections into the dural sinuses (of Pacchioni) through which CSF returns to the blood.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the tufts pushing into the sinus that absorb CSF.
Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow midline cavity between the two thalami.

title: Lymph from the lower lip, chin and apex of the tongue drains first into which nodes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Lymph from the lower lip, chin and apex of the tongue drains first into which nodes?
body.explanation: The upper face drains to preauricular (parotid) nodes, the central face, cheeks and lateral nose to submandibular nodes, and the lower lip and chin to submental nodes.

title: Which air channels does the lateral nasal wall contain? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which air channels does the lateral nasal wall contain? (choose all)
body.explanation: The conchae divide each nasal cavity into four air channels: the inferior, middle and superior meatuses and the spheno-ethmoidal recess. The ethmoidal labyrinth is the honeycomb of air cells in the ethmoid bone, and the pterygopalatine fossa lies outside the nasal cavity.

title: If clear fluid drips into the orbital cavity after trauma, which wall is likely fractured?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: If clear fluid drips into the orbital cavity after trauma, which wall is likely fractured?
body.explanation: Superior blowout fractures may involve the neighbouring sinus as well as the anterior cranial fossa, presenting with leakage of cerebrospinal fluid.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the grey matter (butterfly). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the deep groove on the front of the cord.
This is at the arrow: the central butterfly-shaped grey area.
Not at the arrow; this is the tiny canal in the middle of the grey matter.
Not at the arrow; this is the motor root leaving the front of the cord.

title: Which fascia lines the deep surface of the pharyngeal muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which fascia lines the deep surface of the pharyngeal muscles?
body.explanation: The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the lateral (outer) surface of the constrictor muscles; the pharyngobasilar fascia lines their deep surface.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
options: Lateral horn (T1 to L2, S2 to S4)
body.explanation: The arrow points to the lateral horn (t1 to l2, s2 to s4). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the small side horn of autonomic neurons.
Not at the arrow; this is the broad front horn of motor neurons.
Not at the arrow; this is the tiny canal in the middle of the grey matter.
Not at the arrow; this is the motor root leaving the front of the cord.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Cochlea: the snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear.
option_notes: Facial nerve (VII) is the nerve running through the temporal bone in its own canal, close to the middle ear.
Incus is the middle ossicle, between malleus and stapes.
Vestibule and semicircular canals is the balance part of the bony labyrinth: the central vestibule and the three looped canals.
The snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear.

title: How does the external carotid artery lie in relation to the internal carotid at its origin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How does the external carotid artery lie in relation to the internal carotid at its origin?
body.explanation: At the origin the external carotid lies anterior and medial to the internal carotid. As it ascends it passes backward and lateral, so higher up it is lateral to the internal carotid.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the parietal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of which two veins?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The retromandibular vein is formed by the union of which two veins?
options: Occipital and posterior auricular veins, at the jaw
body.explanation: On leaving the parotid gland it divides: its anterior division joins the facial vein to form the common facial vein, and its posterior division joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.

title: What does the spinal canal contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the spinal canal contain?
body.explanation: The canal contains the cord, meninges, vessels, nerve roots and surrounding fatty tissue. The discs and pedicles form its walls.
option_notes: Yes.
Yes.
The discs are between bodies.
The pedicles are its walls.

title: Which three components make up the lens, histologically?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which three components make up the lens, histologically?
options: Capsule, zonules and the ciliary processes behind
Capsule, subcapsular epithelium and lens fibres
body.explanation: The lens is a biconvex structure of great elasticity, lost with age as the lens hardens. Its three components are the capsule, the subcapsular epithelium (only on the anterior surface) and the lens fibres, filled with crystallins.

title: Each spinal segment supplies a specific skin area. What is this area called?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Each spinal segment supplies a specific skin area. What is this area called?
body.explanation: Each segment corresponds to a dermatome (skin area) and a myotome (muscles).
option_notes: Dermatome: skin area.
Myotome: muscles.
Sclerotome is embryonic bone tissue.
Not the term used.

title: What protects the central nervous system?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What protects the central nervous system?
body.explanation: The CNS is encased in bone (skull and spine), reinforced by the meninges and cushioned by CSF.
option_notes: Bony protection.
The meninges reinforce it.
CSF cushions it.
Ganglia are PNS structures, not protection.

title: Which muscles are supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, according to the lecture? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles are supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, according to the lecture? (choose all)
body.explanation: The lecture lists the buccal branch as supplying the orbicularis oris, buccinator and zygomaticus. The temporalis is a muscle of mastication (V3) and the platysma takes the cervical branch.

title: What is the anteroposterior diameter of the spinal canal in the lumbar region?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the anteroposterior diameter of the spinal canal in the lumbar region?
body.explanation: The canal measures 12 to 22 mm in the cervical region and 22 to 25 mm in the lumbar region.
option_notes: Lumbar canal diameter.
That is the cervical range.
Too small.
Too large.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Incus: the middle ossicle, between malleus and stapes.
option_notes: Vestibule and semicircular canals is the balance part of the bony labyrinth: the central vestibule and the three looped canals.
Facial nerve (VII) is the nerve running through the temporal bone in its own canal, close to the middle ear.
The middle ossicle, between malleus and stapes.
Cochlea is the snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear.

title: Where does CSF go back into the blood?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does CSF go back into the blood?
options: Through the arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses
Through the choroid plexus into the arteries
Directly through the pia into the brain tissue
Through the central canal into the spinal veins
body.explanation: CSF passes into the venous circulation through arachnoid granulations that project into the dural sinuses, especially the superior sagittal sinus.
option_notes: Arachnoid granulations drain CSF into the sinuses.
The choroid plexus produces CSF.
Not the main route.
Not the main route.

title: Which nerve can be sectioned to control excessive rhinorrhea?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve can be sectioned to control excessive rhinorrhea?
body.explanation: Excessive rhinorrhea due to vasomotor and allergic rhinitis can be controlled by sectioning the Vidian nerve, the nerve of the pterygoid canal.

title: Which fibres does the middle cerebellar peduncle carry?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which fibres does the middle cerebellar peduncle carry?
options: Pontocerebellar fibres from the contralateral pontine nuclei
body.explanation: The middle peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibres from the opposite pontine nuclei, bringing motor plans from the cortex.
option_notes: From the opposite pontine nuclei.
These run in the inferior peduncle.
That is the superior peduncle.
These enter through the inferior peduncle.

title: Where do the parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland synapse?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do the parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland synapse?
body.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in the greater petrosal nerve (a branch of the facial nerve) and then the nerve of the pterygoid canal, before synapsing in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Postganglionic fibres travel with the maxillary nerve and finally the zygomatic nerve.

title: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Lateral ventricle: the C-shaped ventricle in each hemisphere.
option_notes: The C-shaped ventricle in each hemisphere.
Choroid plexus is the vascular tufts in the ventricles that produce CSF.
Cerebral aqueduct is the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
Fourth ventricle is the ventricle between the brainstem and cerebellum.

title: Which artery supplies the lacrimal gland?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery supplies the lacrimal gland?
body.explanation: The lacrimal artery supplies the lacrimal gland, and its terminal branches supply the lateral upper and lower eyelids and the conjunctiva.

title: A tumour blocks the cerebral aqueduct. This causes:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A tumour blocks the cerebral aqueduct. This causes:
options: Communicating hydrocephalus with all four ventricles dilated
Dilation of the fourth ventricle only
Non-communicating hydrocephalus with the lateral and third ventricles dilated
No change because CSF exits through Luschka
body.explanation: Ventricles upstream of the block dilate; the fourth is downstream.
option_notes: The fourth ventricle stays normal.
It lies below the block.
Blocked flow dilates the ventricles above it.
Those openings are below the block.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the utricle. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the smaller, lower sac of the vestibule, joined to the cochlear duct.
This is at the arrow: the larger, upper sac of the vestibule, receiving the canals.
Not at the arrow; this is the vertical canal at the top, facing forward.
Not at the arrow; this is the swelling at one end of each canal, holding the crista.

title: Which extrapyramidal tracts are uncrossed? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which extrapyramidal tracts are uncrossed? (choose all)
body.explanation: Uncrossed: vestibulospinal, olivospinal, reticulospinal. Crossed: rubrospinal, tectospinal.

title: Which is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the largest deep cerebellar nucleus?
body.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral; it is linked to planning and coordination of voluntary movement.
option_notes: The dentate is the largest.
The fastigial is small and medial.
The globose is small.
The emboliform is small.

title: The floor of the fourth ventricle is called:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The floor of the fourth ventricle is called:
body.explanation: Diamond-shaped, on the back of the pons and upper medulla.
option_notes: Part of the roof.
Roof.
The diamond-shaped rhomboid fossa.
Its lower tip.

title: Where is the middle nasal meatus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the middle nasal meatus?
options: Between the inferior concha and the nasal floor
Between the middle and superior conchae
Between the superior concha and the nasal roof
Between the inferior and middle conchae
body.explanation: Inferior meatus: between the inferior concha and the nasal floor. Middle meatus: between the inferior and middle conchae. Superior meatus: between the middle and superior conchae. Spheno-ethmoidal recess: between the superior concha and the nasal roof.

title: Which meningeal layer is the only one to follow the gyri and fissures?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which meningeal layer is the only one to follow the gyri and fissures?
option_notes: The pia dips into every sulcus.
It bridges sulci.
It lines the skull.
Not a meningeal layer.

title: Which is the largest paranasal sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the largest paranasal sinus?
body.explanation: The maxillary sinus lies in the body of the maxilla and is the largest. The maxilla is the only facial bone that contains a paranasal sinus.

title: In the pupillary light reflex, where do the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres originate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In the pupillary light reflex, where do the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres originate?
body.explanation: The preganglionic parasympathetic fibres originate in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and travel in cranial nerve III to the ciliary ganglion. From there postganglionic fibres reach the pupillary constrictor muscle.

title: Which muscle is involved in ptosis, and which nerve supplies it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle is involved in ptosis, and which nerve supplies it?
options: Orbicularis oculi, supplied by CN VII
Superior rectus, supplied by CN IV
Ciliary muscle, supplied by CN VI
body.explanation: Ptosis is drooping of the eyelid. The levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper lid and is supplied by the oculomotor nerve; its smooth superior tarsal part is sympathetic.

title: A patient has a seizure that starts with jerking of one hand. Where is the lesion most likely?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A patient has a seizure that starts with jerking of one hand. Where is the lesion most likely?
body.explanation: Epilepsy is a sign of a cortical lesion; the type of seizure depends on where it is.
option_notes: Seizures come from the cortex.
The cord does not cause seizures.
The cerebellum causes ataxia, not seizures.
Nerves do not cause seizures.

title: Which are extrinsic muscles that elevate the larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are extrinsic muscles that elevate the larynx?
body.explanation: Elevators: thyrohyoid, mylohyoid and digastric. Depressors: sternothyroid, sternohyoid and omohyoid. The extrinsic muscles ensure laryngeal mobility, especially during swallowing.
option_notes: Thyrohyoid raises it.
Mylohyoid raises it via the hyoid.
Sternothyroid lowers it.
Omohyoid lowers it.

title: Which artery mainly supplies the thalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery mainly supplies the thalamus?
body.explanation: The thalamus is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery, in four territories: anterior, inferolateral, paramedian and posterior.
option_notes: Not the main supply.
Not the main supply.
The posterior cerebral artery mainly supplies it.
Only indirectly.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
options: CN IX, X, XI (behind the olive)
body.explanation: The arrow points to the olive. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the top of the brainstem, below the diencephalon.
This is at the arrow: the oval swelling on the side of the upper medulla.
Not at the arrow; this is the nerve rootlets between pyramid and olive.
Not at the arrow; this is the nerve rootlets behind the olive.

title: Which muscles elevate the eyeball? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles elevate the eyeball? (choose all)
body.explanation: Elevation: superior rectus and inferior oblique. Depression: inferior rectus and superior oblique.

title: What forms the posterior wall of the interventricular foramen of Monro?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the posterior wall of the interventricular foramen of Monro?
options: The anterior pole of the thalamus
body.explanation: The anterior pole of the thalamus forms the posterior wall of the foramen of Monro.
option_notes: The narrow front end of the thalamus.
The pulvinar is the back end.
The pineal is at the back of the third ventricle.
The mammillary bodies are on the floor.

title: Which lie on the lower level of the medial wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which lie on the lower level of the medial wall?
body.explanation: Below the facial canal prominence: the promontory, the oval window and the round window. The lateral semicircular canal prominence is above it; the tegmen is the roof.
option_notes: The promontory is on the lower level.
The oval window is on the lower level.
The lateral canal is on the upper level.
The tegmen is the roof.

title: Name the four infrahyoid strap muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the four infrahyoid strap muscles.
body.explanation: Four pairs of strap muscles in a fascial sheath in the anterior neck. They fix or depress the hyoid bone during swallowing and speech, supplied by the anterior rami of the upper three cervical nerves.
option_notes: These are suprahyoid muscles.
These are other neck muscles.
These are laryngeal muscles.
These are the four infrahyoid muscles.

title: Which nerves carry the postganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the pupil?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves carry the postganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the pupil?
options: The long ciliary nerves of the eye
body.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus sends preganglionic fibres along the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion. Its postganglionic fibres, the short ciliary nerves, innervate the sphincter muscle of the pupil.

title: Which functions depend on the reticular formation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functions depend on the reticular formation?
body.explanation: Arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, motor coordination, cardiovascular and respiratory control, pain modulation and habituation.
option_notes: It keeps us awake.
It controls breathing.
The cochlea.
Taste buds and VII, IX, X.

title: What inserts on the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What inserts on the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage?
body.explanation: The anterior angle of the base is extended by the vocal process, which gives insertion to the vocal ligament. The lateral angle bears the muscular process, on which the posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles insert.
option_notes: The vocal ligament inserts on the vocal process.
It inserts on the muscular process.
It joins the two arytenoids.
It inserts on the muscular process.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the lateral geniculate nucleus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What happens to the pupil on parasympathetic stimulation in bright light?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What happens to the pupil on parasympathetic stimulation in bright light?
options: It widens (mydriasis), by the dilator pupillae
It narrows (miosis), by the sphincter pupillae
body.explanation: Light exposure and parasympathetic stimulation narrow the pupil (miosis) via the sphincter pupillae. Darkness and sympathetic stimulation widen it (mydriasis) via the dilator pupillae.

title: Where does the rubrospinal tract begin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the rubrospinal tract begin?
body.explanation: It starts in the red nucleus of the midbrain, crosses immediately and descends contralaterally; thought to help fine hand control.

title: Which cerebellar peduncle is the largest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cerebellar peduncle is the largest?
body.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis) is the largest input pathway to the cerebellum.
option_notes: It is the largest input pathway.
The superior peduncle is mainly output.
The inferior peduncle carries both input and output.
They differ in size.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the medullary pyramid (medulla). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure connects the two cerebellar hemispheres?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure connects the two cerebellar hemispheres?
body.explanation: The two hemispheres are united by a median portion, the vermis.
option_notes: The vermis is the median part joining the hemispheres.
The corpus callosum joins the cerebral hemispheres.
The dentate is a deep nucleus inside each hemisphere.
The middle peduncle joins the cerebellum to the pons.

title: Where do the pyramidal tracts get their name?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do the pyramidal tracts get their name?
options: The shape of the ventral horn
body.explanation: They are named after the medullary pyramids of the medulla oblongata, which they pass through.

title: The blood supply to the orbit comes mainly from which artery?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The blood supply to the orbit comes mainly from which artery?
body.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is the first branch off the internal carotid as it emerges from the cavernous sinus on the medial side of the clinoid process.

title: What are the fields of Forel?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the fields of Forel?
body.explanation: The fields of Forel are fibre bundles connecting the globus pallidus, thalamus and subthalamic nucleus, important for motor signal transmission.
option_notes: Not pineal.
Not hypothalamic.
The zona incerta lies between them.
Bundles of fibres in the subthalamus.

title: Which ligaments of the temporomandibular joint are mentioned in the lecture? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which ligaments of the temporomandibular joint are mentioned in the lecture? (choose all)
body.explanation: The lecture names three extracapsular ligaments: the lateral, sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments. They stabilise the joint.

title: Which processes belong to the maxilla? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which processes belong to the maxilla? (choose all)
body.explanation: The maxilla has four processes: frontal, zygomatic, alveolar and palatine. The pterygoid process belongs to the sphenoid and the petrous part to the temporal bone.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
options: Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere
body.explanation: Superior cerebellar peduncle: the bundle joining the cerebellum to the midbrain; the main cerebellar output.
option_notes: The bundle joining the cerebellum to the midbrain; the main cerebellar output.
Cerebellar tonsil is the rounded part of the inferior hemisphere beside the vermis, above the foramen magnum.
Anterior lobe of the cerebellum is the smaller part of the cerebellar hemisphere in front of the primary fissure.
Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere is the large part of the cerebellar hemisphere behind the primary fissure.

title: What does the pineal gland secrete?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the pineal gland secrete?
body.explanation: Its pinealocytes secrete melatonin in response to darkness, regulating circadian rhythms.
option_notes: Oxytocin comes from the hypothalamus.
From the pituitary.
Melatonin, which sets the sleep-wake rhythm.
From the adrenal.

title: Which opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the maxillary nerve (V2)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which opening in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the maxillary nerve (V2)?
body.explanation: Foramen rotundum carries V2, foramen ovale carries V3 (mandibular nerve), and foramen spinosum carries the middle meningeal vessels. The optic canal is in the lesser wing.

title: Into which structure do the posterior fibres of the buccinator continue?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Into which structure do the posterior fibres of the buccinator continue?
body.explanation: The buccinator arises from the posterior parts of the maxilla and mandible and from the pterygomandibular raphe, which separates it from the superior constrictor of the pharynx.

title: What is the plica fimbriata?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the plica fimbriata?
options: A mucosal fold on the ventral surface
The fold connecting the tongue to the floor
The opening of the submandibular duct
body.explanation: The ventral surface is smooth with no papillae. In the midline anteriorly a mucosal fold, the frenulum, connects the tongue with the floor of the mouth. Lateral to the frenulum the deep lingual vein can be seen through the mucosa, and lateral to that a fold of mucosa forms the plica fimbriata.

title: Through which opening does the maxillary division pass?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Through which opening does the maxillary division pass?
body.explanation: Ophthalmic (sensory): superior orbital fissure. Maxillary (sensory): foramen rotundum. Mandibular (sensory and motor): foramen ovale.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Medulla oblongata: the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.
option_notes: Cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri) is the thick pillar on the front of the midbrain carrying descending fibres.
Midbrain is the top part of the brainstem, between diencephalon and pons.
Pons is the bulging middle part of the brainstem.
The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.

title: Which structures anchor the orbicularis oculi at the eyelid? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures anchor the orbicularis oculi at the eyelid? (choose all)
body.explanation: The lecture names the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments in connection with the orbital part of orbicularis oculi.

title: Which network, spread through the brainstem, keeps us awake and conscious?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which network, spread through the brainstem, keeps us awake and conscious?
body.explanation: The reticular formation coordinates arousal, consciousness, sleep-wake cycles, and cardiovascular and respiratory control.
option_notes: The reticular formation controls arousal and consciousness.
The medial lemniscus carries touch and position sense.
The corticospinal tract is motor.
The peduncles connect to the cerebellum.

title: What are the three parts of the uvea (vascular layer)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the three parts of the uvea (vascular layer)?
options: Cornea, sclera and the limbus between
body.explanation: The uvea or uveal tract lies between the sclera and the retina. Its anterior portion is the iris and ciliary body; its posterior portion is the choroid.

title: How many cerebellar peduncles connect each side of the cerebellum to the brainstem?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many cerebellar peduncles connect each side of the cerebellum to the brainstem?
body.explanation: Three pairs of peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla.
option_notes: Superior, middle and inferior.
There are three on each side.
They are named superior, middle and inferior.
There are three.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the central canal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the outer white columns of fibre tracts.
This is at the arrow: the tiny canal in the middle of the grey matter.
Not at the arrow; this is the shallow groove on the back of the cord.
Not at the arrow; this is the broad front horn of motor neurons.

title: Which sulcus lies between the highlighted gyri?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which sulcus lies between the highlighted gyri?
body.explanation: The parieto-occipital sulcus separates the precuneus (parietal) from the cuneus (occipital).
option_notes: The intraparietal sulcus divides the superior from the inferior parietal lobule.
The calcarine sulcus runs on the medial occipital lobe between cuneus and lingual gyrus.
The cingulate sulcus runs above the cingulate gyrus on the medial surface.
The parieto-occipital sulcus separates the precuneus (parietal) from the cuneus (occipital).

title: What do the intervertebral foramina transmit?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What do the intervertebral foramina transmit?
body.explanation: The pedicles delimit the intervertebral foramina, through which the spinal nerves leave the canal.
option_notes: Spinal nerves exit through them.
Not only arteries.
No.
No.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
options: Opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
body.explanation: Cuneus: the wedge of medial occipital cortex between the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci.
option_notes: Supramarginal gyrus is the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the lateral sulcus.
Angular gyrus is the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.
The wedge of medial occipital cortex between the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci.
Opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus is the back part of the inferior frontal gyrus; with the triangular part it forms Broca's area (dominant side).

title: Which nerves carry taste from the tongue? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves carry taste from the tongue? (choose all)
body.explanation: Taste: the chorda tympani for the anterior two thirds, the glossopharyngeal nerve for the posterior third, and the internal laryngeal nerve of the vagus for the base. The lingual nerve carries general sensation and the hypoglossal nerve is motor.

title: How long is the pharynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How long is the pharynx?
body.explanation: Length 12 to 14 cm. Width 3.5 cm at its base and 1.5 cm at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.

title: How many paranasal air sinuses are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many paranasal air sinuses are there?
body.explanation: There are four paranasal air sinuses: the ethmoidal cells, sphenoidal, maxillary and frontal sinuses. They are invaginations from the nasal cavity that drain into spaces associated with the lateral nasal wall.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the hypothalamus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the gland hanging from the infundibulum in the sella.
Not at the arrow; this is the round swelling behind the infundibulum.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow midline cavity between the two thalami.
This is at the arrow: the region below the thalamus forming the floor of the third ventricle.

title: Which tonsil sits in the nasopharynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tonsil sits in the nasopharynx?
body.explanation: Features of the nasopharynx: the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), the opening of the auditory tube, and the torus tubarius, a raised ridge above the tube opening.

title: Which space contains CSF?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which space contains CSF?
body.explanation: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and the pia, is filled with CSF.
option_notes: Between arachnoid and pia.
Between bone and dura.
Between dura and arachnoid.
Not a CSF space.

title: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Oculomotor nerve (III): leaves the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.
option_notes: Leaves the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.
Optic nerve (II) is runs from the eye to the optic chiasm.
Trigeminal nerve (V) is the large nerve leaving the side of the pons.
Facial nerve (VII) is leaves at the cerebellopontine angle, with VIII.

title: How much of the lateral wall is the tympanic membrane?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How much of the lateral wall is the tympanic membrane?
body.explanation: The lateral wall separates the tympanic cavity from the external acoustic canal and is formed in four fifths by the tympanic membrane.
option_notes: More than half.
More than a third.
A bony rim surrounds it.
The eardrum forms about four fifths of the lateral wall.

title: What lines the outer layer of the eardrum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lines the outer layer of the eardrum?
body.explanation: Three layers: an outer cuticular layer of stratified squamous epithelium, a middle fibrous layer, and an inner mucosal layer of low columnar epithelium.
option_notes: The outer layer continues the canal skin.
The inner layer is mucosa.
Not the outer layer.
Transitional epithelium lines the urinary tract.

title: When do the five secondary vesicles appear?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: When do the five secondary vesicles appear?
body.explanation: Primary vesicles appear in week 4 and the five secondary vesicles in week 5.
option_notes: Week 5.
Neurulation begins in week 3.
Primary vesicles appear in week 4.
Too late.

title: Which bones form the floor of the orbit, the wall most prone to blowout fracture? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which bones form the floor of the orbit, the wall most prone to blowout fracture? (choose all)
body.explanation: Floor: maxilla, zygomatic bone and palatine bone. The frontal bone forms the roof and the sphenoid body part of the medial wall.

title: Which structures are at risk in thyroid surgery?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures are at risk in thyroid surgery?
body.explanation: The lecture stresses that the anatomical relations with the recurrent nerves and the parathyroid glands are the major risks in thyroidectomy.
option_notes: Nerve injury causes hoarseness.
Removing them causes hypocalcaemia.
Not in the neck.
Not near the thyroid.

title: Which belong to the extrapyramidal system? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which belong to the extrapyramidal system? (choose all)
body.explanation: Basal ganglia, cerebellum and brainstem nuclei including the reticular formation, red nucleus and vestibular nuclei. The pyramids and Betz cells are pyramidal.

title: A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus causes what?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus causes what?
body.explanation: Lesions disrupt the inhibition of movement by the internal globus pallidus, producing hemiballismus, wild flinging movements of one side.
option_notes: Violent flinging movements of one side.
Substantia nigra.
Cortex.
Occipital lobe.

title: When does the anterior neuropore close?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: When does the anterior neuropore close?
body.explanation: The anterior neuropore closes around day 25 and the posterior around day 27.
option_notes: Anterior: day 25.
That is the posterior neuropore.
That is when neurulation begins.
Too late.

title: Which muscles tense the vocal cords?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles tense the vocal cords?
body.explanation: Cricothyroid and vocalis tense the vocal cords; the thyroarytenoid relaxes them; the posterior cricoarytenoid abducts them.
option_notes: Cricothyroid tenses.
Vocalis tenses part of the cord.
Thyroarytenoid relaxes.
It abducts.

title: What is hydrocephalus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is hydrocephalus?
options: Abnormal enlargement of the ventricles from disturbed CSF dynamics
A tumour of the choroid plexus only
body.explanation: Hydrocephalus is excess CSF building up within the ventricles, enlarging them.
option_notes: The ventricles enlarge with excess CSF.
That is a subarachnoid haemorrhage.
That is meningitis.
A papilloma is one rare cause, not the definition.

title: Which nerve carries the parasympathetic fibres toward the lacrimal gland after the geniculate ganglion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve carries the parasympathetic fibres toward the lacrimal gland after the geniculate ganglion?
options: The deep petrosal nerve, from the carotid plexus
body.explanation: The pathway runs from the facial nerve through the greater superficial petrosal nerve and the pterygoid canal to the pterygopalatine ganglion, then along the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves to the gland. The deep petrosal nerve carries the sympathetic fibres.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the auditory tube and torus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the cervical plexus (c1 to c5). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What is the bony anterior opening of the nasal cavity called?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the bony anterior opening of the nasal cavity called?
body.explanation: The anterior opening is the bony piriform aperture, circumscribed above by the nasal bones and below and laterally by the frontal process of the maxillary bone. The vestibule lies more anteriorly, with the major alar and septal cartilages.

title: Where do most corticospinal fibres cross?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do most corticospinal fibres cross?
