body.explanation: Your professor's question: the decussation of the pyramids, 75 to 90 percent of corticospinal fibres, marks the lower medulla.
option_notes: Not here.
Pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla.
Not here.
Only a few cross there.

title: Glaucoma damages which structure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Glaucoma damages which structure?
body.explanation: Glaucoma is a chronic, progressive eye disease caused by damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual field loss. A major risk factor is eye pressure: an abnormality in the drainage system causes fluid to build up.

title: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve arise?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve arise?
body.explanation: On the left it arises from the vagus below the aortic arch, has a mediastinal course between the trachea and the aortic arch, runs along the oesotracheal angle in front of the left edge of the oesophagus, and passes behind the branches of the inferior thyroid artery.
option_notes: That is the right nerve.
Not here.
The left nerve hooks under the aortic arch.
It arises much lower.

title: Where is the internal capsule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the internal capsule?
body.explanation: Internal capsule: between the thalamus and caudate medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. External: between lentiform and claustrum. Extreme: outside the claustrum.
option_notes: That space is the external capsule.
That is the extreme capsule.
Between the thalamus/caudate and the lentiform nucleus.
Not above it.

title: What is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex?
options: The temporal branch of the facial nerve
body.explanation: Touch on the cornea travels in the ophthalmic branch of V to the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve. The efferent limb is the facial motor nucleus on both sides, through the temporal branch of CN VII, closing the eyes.

title: Which semicircular canal lies in the horizontal plane?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which semicircular canal lies in the horizontal plane?
body.explanation: The anterior and posterior canals lie in vertical planes; the lateral canal lies in the horizontal plane.
option_notes: The anterior canal is vertical.
The posterior canal is vertical.
The lateral canal is horizontal.
The superior (anterior) canal is vertical.

title: Which lobe is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which lobe is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Parietal lobe: behind the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus, in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
option_notes: The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus.
The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus, in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
The occipital lobe lies at the back, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus.
The frontal lobe lies in front of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus.

title: Which muscles adduct the vocal cords?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles adduct the vocal cords?
body.explanation: Adductors: the lateral cricoarytenoids and the transverse arytenoid. The posterior cricoarytenoids are the only abductors. The cricothyroid tenses the cords rather than adducting them.
option_notes: Lateral cricoarytenoid adducts.
Transverse arytenoid adducts.
Posterior cricoarytenoid abducts.
Cricothyroid tenses.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the lateral geniculate nucleus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What is the tree-like pattern seen when the cerebellum is cut?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the tree-like pattern seen when the cerebellum is cut?
options: Arbor vitae: branching white matter surrounded by grey cortex
body.explanation: On section, branching white matter surrounded by grey cortex forms the arbor vitae, the tree of life.
option_notes: The arbor vitae.
The vallecula is the groove on the inferior surface.
The vermis is the median part.
That is an opening in the tentorium.

title: Which is the correct order of the visual pathway?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the correct order of the visual pathway?
options: Optic nerve, tract, chiasm, lateral geniculate nucleus, radiation, cortex
Optic tract, nerve, chiasm, thalamus, cortex
Optic nerve, chiasm, radiation, tract, cortex
Optic nerve, chiasm, tract, geniculate, radiation, cortex
body.explanation: Eye, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus (in the thalamus), optic radiation, primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

title: Where does the pharynx become the oesophagus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the pharynx become the oesophagus?
options: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, level with C4
At the level of the hyoid bone, C3
At the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, level with C6
At the level of the sternal notch, T1
body.explanation: Inferiorly it is continuous with the oesophagus at the level of the lower border of the cricoid cartilage anteriorly and the lower border of C6 posteriorly.

title: Cones serve which type of vision?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Cones serve which type of vision?
options: Scotopic vision: night and dim light
No vision, they are supporting cells
body.explanation: Photopic vision is bright light vision served by cones, with high visual acuity for colours and details, and low sensitivity to light. Scotopic vision is night and dim light vision served by rods, with low acuity, no colour, and great sensitivity to light.

title: Through which part of the internal capsule does the corticospinal tract pass?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Through which part of the internal capsule does the corticospinal tract pass?
body.explanation: The corticospinal fibres descend through the posterior limb, behind the geniculate (corticobulbar) tract, which passes through the genu.

title: What does the superior quadrigeminal brachium connect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the superior quadrigeminal brachium connect?
options: The inferior colliculus and the cochlea
The olive and the spinal cord
The superior colliculus and the retina
body.explanation: The superior brachium links the superior colliculus with the retina, for vision. The inferior brachium carries lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus fibres to the medial geniculate body, for hearing.
option_notes: The inferior brachium is auditory.
Middle peduncle.
Not this.
Superior colliculus to the visual pathway (via the LGB).

title: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Anterior corticospinal tract: the uncrossed motor fibres beside the anterior median fissure.
option_notes: Posterior spinocerebellar tract is unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum, at the edge of the lateral funiculus.
Gracile fasciculus is the medial part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the lower body.
Cuneate fasciculus is the lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.
The uncrossed motor fibres beside the anterior median fissure.

title: Which dural fold lies directly above the cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which dural fold lies directly above the cerebellum?
body.explanation: The cerebellum lies inferior to the tentorium cerebelli; its superior surface is related to it.
option_notes: The tentorium roofs over the cerebellum.
The falx cerebri is between the cerebral hemispheres.
The diaphragma sellae covers the pituitary.
The falx cerebelli lies between the cerebellar hemispheres, not above.

title: Which arteries supply the choroid and ciliary processes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which arteries supply the choroid and ciliary processes?
body.explanation: Short ciliary arteries supply the choroid and ciliary processes. Long ciliary arteries supply the anterior segment and anastomose with the extraocular muscle branches.

title: Which parts form the spinocerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which parts form the spinocerebellum?
options: The vermis and the intermediate zones
body.explanation: The spinocerebellum includes the vermis and the intermediate zones, with the fastigial and interposed nuclei as outputs.
option_notes: Vermis + intermediate zones.
That is the cerebrocerebellum.
That is the vestibulocerebellum.
That is the cerebrocerebellum's output.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the laryngopharynx. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which cells are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cells are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex?
body.explanation: Purkinje cells are the only output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, sending inhibitory signals to the deep nuclei.
option_notes: Purkinje cells carry the cortex's output.
Granule cells are interneurons of the granular layer.
Pyramidal cells are in the cerebral cortex.
Astrocytes are glial cells.

title: Where does the frontal sinus drain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the frontal sinus drain?
body.explanation: The frontal sinus is rudimentary at birth and usually well developed by the age of 7 or 8. It drains onto the lateral wall of the middle meatus via the frontonasal duct.

title: Which Brodmann area is the primary motor cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which Brodmann area is the primary motor cortex?
body.explanation: The voluntary motor cortex occupies the precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4, the ascending frontal gyrus.

title: Which structure connects the brainstem to the cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure connects the brainstem to the cerebellum?
body.explanation: Each part of the brainstem connects to the cerebellum by a pair of cerebellar peduncles: superior, middle and inferior.
option_notes: Three pairs of peduncles.
The corpus callosum joins the hemispheres.
The internal capsule connects cortex and brainstem.
The fornix is a limbic pathway.

title: Which horn of the grey matter contains the motor neurons that supply skeletal muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which horn of the grey matter contains the motor neurons that supply skeletal muscles?
options: None; motor neurons are in the white matter
body.explanation: Ventral horns contain motor neurons sending fibres through the ventral roots to muscles.
option_notes: Ventral horn: motor.
Dorsal horn: sensory.
Lateral horn: autonomic.
Neuron bodies are in the grey matter.

title: Which arteries supply the maxillary sinus? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which arteries supply the maxillary sinus? (choose all)
body.explanation: The maxillary sinus receives blood through branches from the infraorbital and superior alveolar branches of the maxillary arteries. The supratrochlear and anterior ethmoidal arteries supply the frontal and ethmoidal sinuses.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the corpus callosum. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the arched band of fibres joining the hemispheres.
Not at the arrow; this is the top of the brainstem, below the diencephalon.
Not at the arrow; this is the large egg-shaped grey mass beside the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the round swelling behind the infundibulum.

title: Which part of the brain keeps us alive by controlling vital functions?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the brain keeps us alive by controlling vital functions?
body.explanation: The cerebrum thinks, feels and remembers; the brainstem keeps us alive; the cerebellum makes movement smooth; the spinal cord connects and reacts.
option_notes: The brainstem controls vital functions.
The cerebrum thinks and remembers.
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
The cord connects and reacts.

title: Which muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV)?
body.explanation: LR6 SO4: the lateral rectus takes CN VI and the superior oblique takes CN IV. Every other extraocular muscle takes CN III.

title: What is the spinal cord's role in a withdrawal reflex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the spinal cord's role in a withdrawal reflex?
options: It processes the reflex without needing the brain
It only relays the signal to the brain
It has no role; reflexes are cerebellar
body.explanation: The spinal cord processes simple reflexes independently of the brain, such as withdrawal.
option_notes: Simple reflexes are integrated in the cord.
The cord does more than relay.
The cerebellum coordinates, it does not run spinal reflexes.
The cord does not secrete hormones.

title: Where do the ganglion cell fibres synapse before reaching the cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do the ganglion cell fibres synapse before reaching the cortex?
options: The pretectal nucleus, in the dorsal midbrain
body.explanation: The ganglion nerve fibres synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus, a relay centre in the thalamus. The fibres leaving it form the optic radiation.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
options: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
Opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
body.explanation: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus: the middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus, part of Broca's area.
option_notes: Paracentral lobule is the medial continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri (leg area).
Insula is the cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.
The middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus, part of Broca's area.
Opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus is the back part of the inferior frontal gyrus; with the triangular part it forms Broca's area (dominant side).

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the thyroid cartilage. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the complete ring below the thyroid cartilage.
Not at the arrow; this is the forward bulge where the two thyroid laminae meet.
Not at the arrow; this is the leaf-shaped cartilage behind the tongue base.
This is at the arrow: the large shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx (Adam's apple).

title: Which are relations of the sphenoidal sinus laterally? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are relations of the sphenoidal sinus laterally? (choose all)
body.explanation: Laterally: the cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. The pituitary gland lies superiorly and the nasopharynx inferiorly.

title: Which nerve supplies the macula of the saccule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve supplies the macula of the saccule?
body.explanation: The superior vestibular nerve gives the utricular, superior ampullary and lateral ampullary nerves. The inferior vestibular nerve forms the saccular nerve. There is also a posterior ampullary nerve.
option_notes: The superior nerve supplies utricle, anterior and lateral ampullae.
The cochlear nerve is for hearing.
VII is not sensory to the labyrinth.
The inferior vestibular nerve supplies the saccule.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the optic tract. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Where do climbing fibres come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do climbing fibres come from?
options: Only from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus
body.explanation: Climbing fibres arise exclusively from the contralateral inferior olive; each makes hundreds of excitatory synapses on one Purkinje cell.
option_notes: Only the opposite inferior olive.
That is a mossy fibre source.
That is a mossy fibre source.
That is a mossy fibre source.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the pituitary gland (via infundibulum). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the gland hanging from the infundibulum in the sella.
Not at the arrow; this is the small gland at the back of the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the round swelling behind the infundibulum.
Not at the arrow; this is the large egg-shaped grey mass beside the third ventricle.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the temporal fossa: temporalis origin. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What are the cerebellar tonsils?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the cerebellar tonsils?
options: Rounded parts of the medial inferior hemispheres beside the inferior vermis
body.explanation: The tonsils are rounded portions of the medial inferior cerebellar hemispheres, on either side of the inferior vermis.
option_notes: They sit just above the foramen magnum.
Those are the palatine tonsils.
The deep nuclei are inside the white matter.
They are on the inferior surface.

title: Which is the major nerve of the lumbar plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the major nerve of the lumbar plexus?
body.explanation: The lumbar plexus supplies the pelvis and anterior leg; its major nerve is the femoral, whose saphenous branch runs down the anterior lower leg.

title: The pineal gland belongs to which part of the diencephalon?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The pineal gland belongs to which part of the diencephalon?
body.explanation: Your professor's question. The epithalamus includes the habenula, the stria medullaris and the pineal gland.
option_notes: Not thalamic.
The pineal belongs to the epithalamus.
Not hypothalamic.
Not subthalamic.

title: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tract is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Lateral corticospinal tract: the main crossed motor tract, in the lateral funiculus.
option_notes: Cuneate fasciculus is the lateral part of the dorsal column: fine touch and position sense from the upper body.
Lateral spinothalamic tract is pain and temperature, in the lateral funiculus.
The main crossed motor tract, in the lateral funiculus.
Posterior spinocerebellar tract is unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum, at the edge of the lateral funiculus.

title: Which muscle protrudes the tongue?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle protrudes the tongue?
body.explanation: Protrusion: genioglossus on both sides. Retraction: styloglossus and hyoglossus on both sides. Depression: hyoglossus and genioglossus on both sides. Elevation: styloglossus and palatoglossus on both sides.

title: Where do vocal nodules form, and why there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do vocal nodules form, and why there?
options: Along the whole free edge equally
body.explanation: During vibration the area of maximum contact between the cords is at the junction of their anterior one third and posterior two thirds, so it takes the most friction. People who overuse the voice, such as teachers and singers, develop inflammatory nodules there.
option_notes: Not at the commissure.
Not here.
Not along the whole edge.
Junction of anterior and middle thirds, where vibration is greatest.

title: Where is the primary visual cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the primary visual cortex?
options: In the frontal lobe, at the front
body.explanation: The optic radiation relays the signal from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the primary visual cortex within the occipital lobe.

title: What gives the posterior third of the tongue its nodular surface?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What gives the posterior third of the tongue its nodular surface?
body.explanation: The posterior third has no papillae but shows a nodular surface because of the underlying lymphatic nodules, the lingual tonsils.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the frontal sinus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the retina (both eyes). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Where does the thyroid sit in relation to the infrahyoid muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the thyroid sit in relation to the infrahyoid muscles?
body.explanation: It is located in the infrahyoid region in front of the upper end of the trachea and the lower part of the larynx, just behind the infrahyoid muscles.
option_notes: The strap muscles are superficial to it.
Not between them.
It lies just deep to the infrahyoid muscles.
It is below the hyoid.

title: How many extrapyramidal tracts are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many extrapyramidal tracts are there?
body.explanation: Vestibulospinal, olivospinal and reticulospinal (uncrossed) plus rubrospinal and tectospinal (crossed).

title: At what level does the common carotid artery divide into its two terminal branches?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: At what level does the common carotid artery divide into its two terminal branches?
options: Upper border of the thyroid cartilage
Upper border of the hyoid bone, at about C2
Lower border of the cricoid cartilage, at C6
Behind the sternoclavicular joint, at T1
body.explanation: The bifurcation takes place in the carotid triangle, at the level of the upper border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, opposite the disc between C3 and C4.

title: Which glial cells support neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which glial cells support neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia?
body.explanation: Satellite cells support neuronal cell bodies in ganglia and regulate their microenvironment.
option_notes: PNS ganglia.
CNS.
CNS.
CNS.

title: At birth, at which vertebral level does the spinal cord end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: At birth, at which vertebral level does the spinal cord end?
body.explanation: At 6 months of fetal life it reaches S1, at birth L3, and in adults the L1/L2 disc.
option_notes: At birth it ends at L3.
This is the adult level.
This is at 6 months of fetal life.
Too high.

title: Which structure is the relay for the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is the relay for the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
body.explanation: Light enters the pupil and stimulates the retina. Ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve, the nasal fibres cross at the chiasm, and fibres from the optic tracts project to the pretectal nuclei in the dorsal midbrain.

title: Which branches does the facial artery give in the neck? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which branches does the facial artery give in the neck? (choose all)
body.explanation: In the neck the facial artery gives the ascending palatine, tonsillar, submental and glandular branches. The superior labial and angular arteries are given on the face.

title: Why is herniation of the cerebellar tonsils life-threatening?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why is herniation of the cerebellar tonsils life-threatening?
options: It compresses the medulla, threatening breathing and circulation
It tears the middle meningeal artery
It compresses the spinal cord at L1
body.explanation: Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla oblongata, threatening vital respiratory and cardiovascular functions.
option_notes: The medulla holds the respiratory and cardiovascular centres.
The optic nerves are far in front.
That causes an epidural haematoma.
Not at that level.

title: Which nerves supply the frontal sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves supply the frontal sinus?
body.explanation: The frontal sinus is supplied by branches of the supraorbital nerve and supratrochlear nerve from the ophthalmic nerve (V1). Its blood supply comes from branches of the anterior ethmoidal, supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Insula: the cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.
option_notes: Inferior temporal gyrus is the lowest gyrus of the lateral temporal lobe.
Angular gyrus is the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.
The cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.
Superior parietal lobule is the parietal area above the intraparietal sulcus.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Lateral ventricles. Paired C-shaped cavities in the hemispheres: frontal, temporal and occipital horns, body and atrium.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.
This is at the arrow: the paired C-shaped cavities in the hemispheres.

title: Which structures belong to the epithalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures belong to the epithalamus?
body.explanation: Epithalamus: stria medullaris, posterior commissure, habenular nuclei, pineal body and paraventricular nuclei. The mammillary bodies belong to the hypothalamus.
option_notes: Habenula is epithalamus.
Stria medullaris is epithalamus.
Hypothalamus.
Subthalamus.

title: At what age do the sinuses enlarge rapidly?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: At what age do the sinuses enlarge rapidly?
body.explanation: The sinuses are rudimentary or even absent at birth, enlarge rapidly at the age of 6 to 7 years, then again after puberty. They increase in size through enlargement of the bones from birth to adult life, and resorption of bone in old age.

title: Which statement about the cornea is correct?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which statement about the cornea is correct?
options: It is relatively avascular but has a fine vascular plexus
It provides insertion for the extraocular muscles
It is less sensitive than the sclera
body.explanation: The cornea has higher convexity, is completely avascular, is nourished by the lacrimal gland outside and the aqueous humour inside, and is highly sensitive through CN V1.

title: Name the three parts of the bony labyrinth.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the three parts of the bony labyrinth.
body.explanation: The bony labyrinth, derived from the otic capsule, has three parts: the cochlea, the vestibule and the semicircular canals, lined by periosteum and containing perilymph.
option_notes: These are membranous parts.
These are the ossicles.
Cochlea, vestibule and semicircular canals.
These are membranous parts.

title: Which three bones form the roof, front to back?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which three bones form the roof, front to back?
body.explanation: The roof runs anterior (nasal), superior (ethmoidal) and posterior (sphenoidal).

title: Which part of the orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids gently, as in blinking or sleep?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids gently, as in blinking or sleep?
body.explanation: The palpebral part acts involuntarily and closes the lids gently. The orbital part closes the eye forcefully and is under conscious control, wrinkling the forehead.

title: From which embryonic vesicle does the midbrain develop?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: From which embryonic vesicle does the midbrain develop?
body.explanation: Myelencephalon (fifth vesicle) forms the medulla, metencephalon (fourth) the pons, mesencephalon (third) the midbrain.
option_notes: Gives the pons and cerebellum.
Gives the medulla.
Gives the hemispheres.
The mesencephalon becomes the midbrain.

title: Where does the medial geniculate body send its output?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the medial geniculate body send its output?
body.explanation: The MGB receives auditory input from the inferior colliculus and projects to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.
option_notes: The MGB sends hearing to the auditory cortex.
That is from the LGB.
Not its output.
Not its output.

title: Which structures form the roof of the oral cavity proper? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures form the roof of the oral cavity proper? (choose all)
body.explanation: The roof is the hard palate in front and the soft palate behind. The mylohyoid forms the floor, on which the anterior two thirds of the tongue lies.

title: What is the crus commune?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the crus commune?
options: The shared end of two canals
The dilated end of each canal
The duct joining utricle and saccule
body.explanation: The posterior non-ampullated end of the anterior canal unites with the upper non-ampullated end of the posterior canal to form the crus commune, which opens into the vestibule.
option_notes: The anterior and posterior canals share one end.
The dilated end is the ampulla.
That is the utriculo-saccular duct.
That is the cupula or helicotrema.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the occipital lobe. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
Not at the arrow; this is the structure under the occipital lobes, behind the brainstem.
This is at the arrow: the lobe at the back of the hemisphere.
Not at the arrow; this is the lobe behind the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the zygomatic arch: masseter origin. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?
body.explanation: The lecture's mnemonic: 128 are the sensory nerves; 3, 4, 6, 11 and 12 are the motor nerves; 5, 7, 9 and 10 are mixed. Parasympathetic fibres run in 3, 7, 9 and 10.

title: Which space holds fat and the venous plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which space holds fat and the venous plexus?
body.explanation: Your professor's own quiz question: the epidural space, outside the dura, contains fat and the venous plexus.
option_notes: CSF.
A potential space.
CSF in the cord.
The epidural space holds fat and veins.

title: Where does the larynx sit in children compared with adults?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the larynx sit in children compared with adults?
body.explanation: The position varies with age: it is higher in children (C2 to C3) than in adults. In newborns it is in contact with the veil, which is why they keep exclusive nasal breathing until about four months.
option_notes: The child's larynx is higher, not lower.
It is higher in children.
It is predictably higher.
In children it sits higher, about C2 to C3.

title: Which segments contain the lateral horns, the source of sympathetic outflow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which segments contain the lateral horns, the source of sympathetic outflow?
body.explanation: Lateral horns are in T1 to L2 (sympathetic) and S2 to S4 (parasympathetic).
option_notes: Thoracolumbar: sympathetic.
Not cervical.
Not this range.
S2 to S4 is parasympathetic, not sympathetic.

title: From front to back, the floor of the third ventricle is formed by:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: From front to back, the floor of the third ventricle is formed by:
options: Mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, infundibulum, optic chiasm
Infundibulum, optic chiasm, mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum
Lamina terminalis, pineal gland, posterior commissure, habenula
Optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies
option_notes: Reversed.
Wrong order.
That is the back wall area.
Optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies.

title: Which are features of the non-visual retina? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are features of the non-visual retina? (choose all)
options: It is not sensitive to light
It covers the ciliary body and the back of the iris
It is where the optic nerve leaves
body.explanation: The non-visual retina is the portion not sensitive to light: the anterior continuation of the pigment cell layer plus supporting cells over the ciliary body and the posterior surface of the iris.

title: Name the three cavities of the middle ear.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the three cavities of the middle ear.
body.explanation: The middle ear is an air cavity in the temporal bone: a central tympanic cavity, continued behind by the mastoid cells and forward by the Eustachian tube.
option_notes: These are inner ear parts.
These are external ear parts.
Eustachian tube, tympanic cavity and mastoid spaces.
Windows are openings, not cavities.

title: Which fissure separates the anterior and posterior lobes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which fissure separates the anterior and posterior lobes?
body.explanation: The primary fissure divides the smaller anterior lobe from the larger posterior lobe.
option_notes: The primary fissure.
This separates the posterior and flocculonodular lobes.
This separates the cerebral hemispheres.
This is in the cerebrum.

title: Where is the primary visual cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the primary visual cortex?
body.explanation: The primary visual cortex, V1 or area 17, lies around the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe.

title: How many sets of ethmoidal air cells are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many sets of ethmoidal air cells are there?
options: Two: anterior and posterior only, no middle
body.explanation: The ethmoidal sinus is composed of three sets of ethmoidal air cells: anterior, middle and posterior. There are 3 to 18 ethmoid air cells on each side.

title: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Abducens nerve (VI): leaves at the pontomedullary junction, near the midline.
option_notes: Hypoglossal nerve (XII) is leaves the medulla between the pyramid and the olive.
Leaves at the pontomedullary junction, near the midline.
Facial nerve (VII) is leaves at the cerebellopontine angle, with VIII.
Optic nerve (II) is runs from the eye to the optic chiasm.

title: Which glial cells line the ventricles and help produce CSF?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which glial cells line the ventricles and help produce CSF?
body.explanation: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and produce and circulate CSF.
option_notes: They line the ventricles.
Astrocytes form part of the blood-brain barrier.
Schwann cells are in the PNS.
Microglia are immune cells.

title: Where are the lateral horns found?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where are the lateral horns found?
options: T1 to L2 and S2 to S4
body.explanation: Lateral horns lie in T1 to L2 for sympathetic outflow and in S2 to S4 for parasympathetic outflow.
option_notes: Sympathetic T1 to L2 and parasympathetic S2 to S4.
Not cervical.
Not every segment.
Not this range.

title: Which motor neurons of the anterior horn supply the limbs?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which motor neurons of the anterior horn supply the limbs?
body.explanation: In the ventral horn the lateral group supplies the limbs; the medial group the trunk, head and neck.
option_notes: Supplies the trunk.
The lateral group supplies the limbs.
Not motor.
Not this.

title: Which structures lie superior to the sphenoidal sinus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures lie superior to the sphenoidal sinus?
options: The cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery
body.explanation: Relations: superior, the hypophyseal fossa, pituitary gland and optic chiasma; inferior, the nasopharynx and pterygoid canal; medial, the other sphenoid bone; lateral, the cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.

title: How many cranial nerves arise from nuclei in the brainstem?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many cranial nerves arise from nuclei in the brainstem?
body.explanation: Ten of the twelve cranial nerves arise from brainstem nuclei. The optic and olfactory nerves are the exceptions.
option_notes: I and II do not arise from the brainstem.
Too few.
Ten: III to XII.
Too few.

title: What shape is the grey matter in cross-section?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What shape is the grey matter in cross-section?
body.explanation: Central grey matter shaped like a butterfly or H, with four wings, the horns, surrounded by peripheral white matter.
option_notes: No.
No.
No.
A butterfly or H shape.

title: Which nerves emerge from the ventral surface of the pons?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerves emerge from the ventral surface of the pons?
body.explanation: CN V from the mid-pons, CN VI, VII and VIII from the pontomedullary region. CN IV emerges dorsally; CN XII from the medulla.
option_notes: V from the side of the pons.
VI at the lower pons.
IV leaves behind.
XII from the medulla.

title: Which cartilages are unpaired?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cartilages are unpaired?
body.explanation: The unpaired cartilages are large: thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis. The paired ones are small: arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform.
option_notes: These are paired.
Thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis are single.
The arytenoid is paired.
Corniculate and cuneiform are paired.

title: Where does the parotid duct open?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the parotid duct open?
options: Under the tongue, at the sublingual papilla
Into the floor of the nose
body.explanation: A small papilla on the mucosa opposite the upper second molar tooth marks the opening of the duct of the parotid gland.

title: Where does the external carotid artery end, and into what?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the external carotid artery end, and into what?
options: In the carotid triangle, as the facial and lingual arteries
At the base of the skull, entering the carotid canal to reach the brain and its branches
Behind the mandible, as the occipital artery
In the parotid gland, as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries
body.explanation: It terminates in the substance of the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible, dividing into its two terminal branches: the superficial temporal and the maxillary arteries.

title: What do gamma motor neurons supply?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What do gamma motor neurons supply?
body.explanation: Alpha motor neurons, the largest in the nervous system, supply skeletal muscle; gamma motor neurons supply the intrafusal fibres of the muscle spindle.

title: Which receptors serve balance?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which receptors serve balance?
body.explanation: Maculae of the utricle and saccule serve static balance; cristae ampullaris of the semicircular ducts serve kinetic balance. The organ of Corti serves hearing.
option_notes: Maculae sense static balance.
Cristae sense rotation.
The organ of Corti is for hearing.
The stria makes endolymph.

title: How long is the external auditory canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How long is the external auditory canal?
body.explanation: A cylindrical canal closed internally by the tympanic membrane: length 25 mm, average width 8 mm, with an elongated S-shaped course.
option_notes: Too short.
Too short.
Too long.
The canal is about 25 mm long.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the cerebral peduncles. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the oval swelling on the side of the upper medulla.
Not at the arrow; this is the nerve at the pontomedullary junction near the midline.
Not at the arrow; this is the nerves at the angle between pons, medulla and cerebellum.
This is at the arrow: the two thick pillars on the front of the midbrain.

title: Which nerve contributes Jacobson's nerve to the tympanic plexus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve contributes Jacobson's nerve to the tympanic plexus?
body.explanation: The tympanic plexus on the promontory is formed by the tympanic branch of CN IX (Jacobson's nerve), sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus and a branch from the geniculate ganglion.
option_notes: VII gives the chorda tympani.
Jacobson's nerve is the tympanic branch of IX.
X gives Arnold's nerve to the ear canal.
V is not the source.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the superior concha. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the external auditory canal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is air spaces in the mastoid behind the middle ear.
This is at the arrow: the S-shaped canal from the concha to the eardrum.
Not at the arrow; this is the membrane-covered opening below the oval window.
Not at the arrow; this is the outer ossicle, its handle attached to the eardrum.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the cornea. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Inferior temporal gyrus: the lowest gyrus of the lateral temporal lobe.
option_notes: The lowest gyrus of the lateral temporal lobe.
Superior temporal gyrus is the top gyrus of the temporal lobe, under the lateral sulcus; its back part holds Wernicke's area.
Temporal pole is the front tip of the temporal lobe.
Insula is the cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the opercula.

title: How many pairs of cervical spinal nerves are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many pairs of cervical spinal nerves are there?
body.explanation: There are 8 cervical pairs although there are only 7 cervical vertebrae.
option_notes: 8 cervical nerve pairs.
7 is the number of cervical vertebrae.
12 is the thoracic count.
5 is the lumbar or sacral count.

title: What forms the floor of the fourth ventricle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the floor of the fourth ventricle?
body.explanation: The floor is the rhomboid fossa, a diamond-shaped depression on the back of the pons and upper medulla. The roof is the superior and inferior medullary vela.
option_notes: Roof.
Lateral walls.
The rhomboid fossa forms the floor.
Roof.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Stapes: the smallest ossicle, its footplate in the oval window.
option_notes: The smallest ossicle, its footplate in the oval window.
Tympanic membrane is the eardrum, closing the inner end of the external auditory canal.
Malleus is the outer ossicle, its handle attached to the eardrum.
Incus is the middle ossicle, between malleus and stapes.

title: What are the main functions of the spinal cord?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the main functions of the spinal cord?
body.explanation: Conduction, reflex activity and autonomic control.
option_notes: It conducts signals up and down.
It handles reflexes.
No hormones.
Choroid plexuses make CSF.

title: What are these forgotten triangles useful for? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are these forgotten triangles useful for? (choose all)
body.explanation: The paper concludes that these triangles are reliable and constant landmarks for identifying the common carotid artery, ligating the lingual artery, identifying the hypoglossal nerve and recognising the common facial vein.

title: What is the average weight of the thyroid gland?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the average weight of the thyroid gland?
body.explanation: Height of the lateral lobes 6 cm, width 6 cm between their lateral edges, isthmus 1 cm wide by 1.5 cm high, weight about 30 g. It is variable, and the gland is bigger in women than in men.
option_notes: Too light.
This is a goitre size.
Far too heavy.
About 30 g in an adult.

title: How does the subthalamic nucleus normally act on movement?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How does the subthalamic nucleus normally act on movement?
options: It excites the internal globus pallidus, which inhibits the thalamus and movement
It directly excites the motor cortex
It releases dopamine into the striatum
It inhibits the internal globus pallidus
body.explanation: Glutamatergic STN neurons increase activity of the GABAergic internal pallidus, which reduces thalamic activity and inhibits movement.
option_notes: This is the circuit; losing it releases movement (hemiballismus).
It does not project to the cortex directly.
Dopamine comes from the substantia nigra.
It excites, not inhibits, the internal pallidus.

title: Which cranial nerves supply the extraocular muscles? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerves supply the extraocular muscles? (choose all)
body.explanation: CN III, IV and VI supply the extraocular muscles. CN II is purely sensory for vision, and CN VII supplies the muscles of facial expression, including the orbicularis oculi.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the choroid (uvea). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which ventral horn motor neurons supply distal muscles?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which ventral horn motor neurons supply distal muscles?
body.explanation: Motor neurons are arranged somatotopically: medial ones supply proximal muscles, lateral ones distal muscles.

title: Why is the thalamus called the gateway to the cortex?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why is the thalamus called the gateway to the cortex?
options: It sits at the entrance of the skull
body.explanation: Every sensation except smell is filtered in the thalamus before reaching the cortex, so it controls what the cortex receives.
option_notes: Choroid plexuses make CSF.
Almost all sensation relays there before the cortex.
Not the reason.
Not motor cortex.

title: Which concha is an independent bone?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which concha is an independent bone?
body.explanation: The inferior turbinate is an independent bone, the most extended and elongated. The superior and middle turbinates detach from the medial aspect of the ethmoid.

title: What happens to the lens for far vision, at rest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What happens to the lens for far vision, at rest?
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens
The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes more convex
The lens moves forward toward the cornea
The pupil constricts and the lens thickens
body.explanation: Far vision, at rest: the ciliary muscles are relaxed and the ligaments are taut (tense), so the lens is flat. Near vision: the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments relax and the lens becomes convex.

title: What role do the outer hair cells play?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What role do the outer hair cells play?
options: They are the true sensory receptors
body.explanation: Outer hair cells are not true sensory receptors: they have contractile properties, react to sound excitation and increase frequency selectivity, modulating the inner hair cells.
option_notes: The inner hair cells are the true receptors.
The stria vascularis makes endolymph.
They amplify and sharpen tuning.
The stapes closes the oval window.

title: What does the tectospinal tract coordinate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the tectospinal tract coordinate?
body.explanation: It begins at the superior colliculus, which receives optic input, crosses quickly and ends at cervical levels.

title: Which arteries supply the cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which arteries supply the cerebellum?
body.explanation: The cerebellum receives three paired arteries: SCA, AICA and PICA.
option_notes: SCA, from the basilar artery.
AICA, from the basilar artery.
PICA, from the vertebral artery.
The MCA supplies the lateral cerebral hemisphere.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the phrenic nerve (to the diaphragm). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the sternocleidomastoid (scm). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What is the main role of climbing fibres?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the main role of climbing fibres?
options: Signalling movement errors for motor learning
Carrying the cortex's output to the thalamus
body.explanation: Climbing fibres are critical for motor learning, signalling errors in movement execution so the cerebellum can refine commands.
option_notes: Error signals for motor learning.
That is the dentate output.
The choroid plexus makes CSF.
That is the spinothalamic tract.

title: What closes the round window?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What closes the round window?
options: The annular ligament of the stapes
body.explanation: The fenestra cochleae (round window) opens into the tympanic cavity below and behind the promontory and is closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
option_notes: The secondary tympanic membrane closes it.
The stapes closes the oval window.
The annular ligament holds the stapes.
The tegmen is the roof.

title: Which are features of nystagmus, according to the lecture? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are features of nystagmus, according to the lecture? (choose all)
body.explanation: Nystagmus often results in reduced vision and depth perception and can affect balance and coordination. The movements can be side to side, up and down, or circular.

title: What does the great circumferential (horizontal) sulcus of Vicq d'Azyr separate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the great circumferential (horizontal) sulcus of Vicq d'Azyr separate?
options: The superior surface from the inferior surface
The anterior lobe from the posterior lobe
The posterior lobe from the flocculonodular lobe
body.explanation: The horizontal fissure separates the superior and inferior surfaces.
option_notes: Superior from inferior surface.
That is the primary fissure.
That is the posterolateral fissure.
Not a fissure function.

title: What forms the medial wall of the occipital horn?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the medial wall of the occipital horn?
options: The bulb of the corpus callosum and the calcar avis
The head of the caudate nucleus
body.explanation: The bulb of the corpus callosum and the calcar avis form its medial wall; the tapetum forms its roof and lateral wall.
option_notes: Medial wall.
Roof and lateral wall.
Medial wall of the frontal horn.
Lateral wall of the frontal horn.

title: What lies posterior to the pharynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lies posterior to the pharynx?
options: The carotid sheath of the neck
body.explanation: The pharynx is separated from the prevertebral fascia only by a layer of loose areolar tissue, which allows it to slide freely on the fascia during swallowing.

title: In the floor of the fourth ventricle, motor nuclei lie:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In the floor of the fourth ventricle, motor nuclei lie:
body.explanation: Medial eminence = motor; vestibular area = sensory.
option_notes: Motor (basal plate) nuclei lie medial.
Sensory nuclei lie lateral.
Sensory (VIII).
Not in the roof.

title: Which muscles are elevators of the pharynx? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles are elevators of the pharynx? (choose all)
body.explanation: The three elevators (longitudinal muscles) are stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus. The constrictors are the circular layer.

title: As it enters the face, the facial artery curves upward over which structure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: As it enters the face, the facial artery curves upward over which structure?
options: The zygomatic arch, behind the orbit
The angle of the mandible, running behind the masseter
The lower border of the maxilla, close beside the nose
The body of the mandible, at the masseter's border
body.explanation: The facial artery passes over the mandible's body along the masseter's anterior border, deep to the platysma, then takes a tortuous course toward the angle of the mouth.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the thalamus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the round swelling behind the infundibulum.
This is at the arrow: the large egg-shaped grey mass beside the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the top of the brainstem, below the diencephalon.
Not at the arrow; this is the region below the thalamus, beside the hypothalamus.

title: Which nerve carries sensation from the cornea?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve carries sensation from the cornea?
body.explanation: The cornea is highly sensitive and its sensation is carried by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the saccule. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the stapes footplate.
Not at the arrow; this is the duct from the vestibule ending in a sac under the dura.
This is at the arrow: the smaller, lower sac of the vestibule, joined to the cochlear duct.
Not at the arrow; this is the vertical canal facing backward.

title: Which changes happen in the near response? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which changes happen in the near response? (choose all)
body.explanation: The near response: accommodation of the lens (the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligament relaxes, the lens becomes more convex), changes in the pupil, and convergence of the eyes.

title: What happens in the second stage of deglutition? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What happens in the second stage of deglutition? (choose all)
options: The aryepiglottic folds close the laryngeal inlet
The bolus is formed by the tongue
Peristalsis carries the bolus to the stomach
body.explanation: The second stage is rapid and involuntary: the nasopharyngeal isthmus closes, the laryngeal inlet closes, and the pharynx and larynx are elevated as the bolus passes from oropharynx to laryngopharynx.

title: Where is the primary sensory area for touch, pain and temperature?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the primary sensory area for touch, pain and temperature?
options: The postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
The precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
body.explanation: The parietal lobe holds the sensory strip, just behind the central sulcus.
option_notes: The sensory strip lies behind the central sulcus.
That is the motor strip.
That is for hearing and language.
That is the visual cortex.

title: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): leaves the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.
option_notes: Optic nerve (II) is runs from the eye to the optic chiasm.
Oculomotor nerve (III) is leaves the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.
Leaves the medulla behind the olive, above the vagus.
Vagus nerve (X) is leaves the medulla behind the olive, below IX.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Fourth ventricle. Tent-shaped cavity behind the pons and medulla, in front of the cerebellum.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the vascular tufts in the ventricles that make CSF.
This is at the arrow: the cavity between the brainstem and cerebellum.
Not at the arrow; this is the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.
Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.

title: What does the Eustachian tube connect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the Eustachian tube connect?
options: The middle ear and the inner ear
The external canal and the cavity
body.explanation: An osseocartilaginous tube running downwards, forwards and medially from the tympanic cavity to the nasopharynx. It equalises air pressure on both sides of the drum.
option_notes: The windows connect middle and inner ear.
The eardrum separates them.
Not this connection.
It links the middle ear to the nasopharynx.

title: Which functions belong to the frontal lobe?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functions belong to the frontal lobe?
body.explanation: Frontal: personality, judgement, planning, speech production, movement and intelligence. Vision is occipital; hearing temporal.
option_notes: The prefrontal cortex governs personality.
Broca is in the frontal lobe.
Vision is occipital.
Hearing is temporal.

title: Which functions are attributed to the insula?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functions are attributed to the insula?
options: Autonomic control of heart rate and blood pressure
body.explanation: The insula handles taste, visceral sensation, autonomic regulation, interoception and parts of speech articulation and swallowing.
option_notes: Taste and visceral sensation are insular.
The insula helps regulate heart rate, blood pressure and digestion.
Vision is occipital.
Language understanding is Wernicke's area.

title: Where are the sphincter pupillae muscles located?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where are the sphincter pupillae muscles located?
body.explanation: The iris is a pigmented diaphragm with a central aperture, the pupil, on the anterior surface of the lens. Sphincter muscles within it adjust pupil size in response to light and the autonomic nervous system.

title: What proportion of pyramidal fibres decussate in the lower medulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What proportion of pyramidal fibres decussate in the lower medulla?
body.explanation: Most pyramidal fibres (75 to 90%) cross in the pyramidal decussation; the rest descend uncrossed.
option_notes: Most, but not all, cross here.
Too few.
Too few.
Some fibres stay uncrossed.

title: A patient has a right facial palsy with weakness of the left arm and leg. What kind of lesion is this?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A patient has a right facial palsy with weakness of the left arm and leg. What kind of lesion is this?
options: An alternating (crossed) syndrome from a brainstem lesion
A lesion of the left motor cortex
body.explanation: A cranial nerve palsy on one side with hemiplegia on the other side is an alternating syndrome; it locates the lesion in the brainstem.
option_notes: Cranial nerve on one side, body on the other: brainstem.
A cortical lesion would not give a peripheral facial palsy on the opposite side.
The cord has no cranial nerves.
The cerebellum gives ataxia, not paralysis.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
options: Lateral horn (T1 to L2, S2 to S4)
body.explanation: The arrow points to the white matter (funiculi). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the outer white columns of fibre tracts.
Not at the arrow; this is the central butterfly-shaped grey area.
Not at the arrow; this is the small side horn of autonomic neurons.
Not at the arrow; this is the sensory root with its swelling, entering at the back.

title: Which structure produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure produces most of the cerebrospinal fluid?
body.explanation: The choroid plexus is the primary source of CSF, producing about 500 mL per day.
option_notes: The choroid plexus makes CSF.
Arachnoid granulations absorb CSF.
The pia covers the brain surface.
The dura is the outer protective layer.

title: Which stage of swallowing is voluntary?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which stage of swallowing is voluntary?
options: The second stage, in the pharynx
The third stage, in the oesophagus
The first stage, in the mouth
body.explanation: Deglutition has three successive stages: the first in the mouth is voluntary, the second in the pharynx and the third in the oesophagus are involuntary.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Pons: the bulging middle part of the brainstem.
option_notes: Medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord.
The bulging middle part of the brainstem.
Superior colliculus is the upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.
Cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri) is the thick pillar on the front of the midbrain carrying descending fibres.

title: Which lobe interprets vision?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which lobe interprets vision?
body.explanation: The occipital lobe interprets vision: colour, light and movement.
option_notes: The occipital lobe is the visual lobe.
The frontal lobe handles movement, speech and personality.
The temporal lobe handles hearing, memory and understanding language.
The parietal lobe handles touch and spatial perception.

title: Trace the afferent limb of the accommodation reflex.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Trace the afferent limb of the accommodation reflex.
options: Retina, optic nerve, pretectal nucleus, Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Cornea, ophthalmic nerve, spinal nucleus of V
Retina, optic nerve, tract, geniculate, cortex
Ciliary muscle, ciliary ganglion, oculomotor nerve
body.explanation: Afferent: retina, optic nerve, optic chiasma, optic tract, lateral geniculate body, visual cortex. Efferent: oculomotor nucleus, parasympathetic fibres, ciliary ganglion, ciliary muscle and circular pupillary muscle.

title: Which sulcus lies between the highlighted gyri?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which sulcus lies between the highlighted gyri?
body.explanation: The calcarine sulcus runs between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; its banks are the primary visual cortex.
option_notes: The calcarine sulcus runs between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; its banks are the primary visual cortex.
The central sulcus (Rolando) separates the frontal and parietal lobes on the lateral surface.
The lateral sulcus (Sylvius) separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
The parieto-occipital sulcus separates the parietal and occipital lobes on the medial surface.

title: Which secondary vesicle becomes the pons and cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which secondary vesicle becomes the pons and cerebellum?
body.explanation: The rhombencephalon divides into the metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla).
option_notes: Pons and cerebellum.
It becomes the medulla.
It becomes the thalamus and hypothalamus.
It becomes the cerebral hemispheres.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the inferior concha. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Where does the spinal cord begin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the spinal cord begin?
options: At the foramen magnum, continuing the medulla
At the atlas, below the foramen magnum by 5 cm
body.explanation: The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum, where it continues the medulla oblongata.
option_notes: It begins at the foramen magnum.
C7 is within the cervical cord.
The pons is above the medulla.
It starts right at the foramen magnum.

title: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Cerebral aqueduct: the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
option_notes: The narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
Fourth ventricle is the ventricle between the brainstem and cerebellum.
Choroid plexus is the vascular tufts in the ventricles that produce CSF.
Third ventricle is the narrow midline ventricle between the two thalami.

title: What is the main content of the submandibular triangle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the main content of the submandibular triangle?
body.explanation: The submandibular gland is the main content of the triangle and lies in its anterior part, superficial to which is the anterior facial vein.

title: From where do all four rectus muscles arise?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: From where do all four rectus muscles arise?
options: The common ring tendon (annulus of Zinn)
The body of the sphenoid, at the apex
The orbital surface of the maxilla, in front
body.explanation: All four recti arise from the common ring tendon at the orbital apex. The superior oblique arises from the body of the sphenoid and the inferior oblique from the anterior part of the floor of the orbit.

title: Into which three topographic portions is the lateral wall divided?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Into which three topographic portions is the lateral wall divided?
body.explanation: Anterior pre-turbinal area, the turbinal area (bony projections, the conchae or turbinates, and the meatuses), and the posterior retroturbinal area.

title: What share of the hemisphere does the frontal lobe make up?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What share of the hemisphere does the frontal lobe make up?
body.explanation: The frontal lobe is about 40 percent of the hemisphere's weight, in front of the central sulcus, with four gyri.
option_notes: Too small.
Too small.
The frontal lobe is about 40% of the hemisphere.
Too large.

title: Where does the superior thyroid artery come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the superior thyroid artery come from?
options: It is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk
It arises from the subclavian artery
It is a branch of the common carotid
body.explanation: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid. It ends at the top of the lateral lobe, dividing into a lateral branch, a medial branch joining the upper border of the isthmus, and a posterior branch.
option_notes: First branch of the external carotid.
That gives the inferior thyroid artery.
Not directly.
Not usually.

title: What separates the cerebellum from the pons and medulla in front of it?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What separates the cerebellum from the pons and medulla in front of it?
body.explanation: The cerebellum is separated from the pons and medulla by the cavity of the fourth ventricle.
option_notes: The fourth ventricle lies between them.
The third ventricle is in the diencephalon.
The tentorium lies above the cerebellum.
The falx lies between the cerebral hemispheres.

title: What is the foramen cecum a remnant of?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the foramen cecum a remnant of?
body.explanation: The foramen cecum is an embryological remnant marking the site of the upper end of the thyroglossal duct.

title: What is the palatine aponeurosis?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the palatine aponeurosis?
options: A muscle of the soft palate
A fibrous sheath of the soft palate
A fold of mucosa beneath the tongue
The bony plate of the hard palate
body.explanation: The palatine aponeurosis is a fibrous sheath attached to the posterior border of the hard palate. It is the expanded tendon of tensor veli palatini, and it splits to enclose the musculus uvulae and gives origin and insertion to the palatine muscles.

title: Which functional area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functional area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: The transverse temporal gyri (Heschl) are the primary auditory cortex.
option_notes: Primary motor cortex lies in the precentral gyrus.
Primary auditory cortex lies in the transverse temporal gyri (Heschl).
Broca's area (speech production) lies in the opercular and triangular parts of the inferior frontal gyrus.
Primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus.

title: Where do the scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do the scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate?
body.explanation: They communicate at the apex of the cochlea through a small opening, the helicotrema.
option_notes: The round window ends the scala tympani.
The oval window opens into the vestibule.
Not the base.
They join at the apex, through the helicotrema.

title: Which muscle is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
body.explanation: The stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by CN IX. The salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus take the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus.

title: What is the transverse diameter of the spinal cord?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the transverse diameter of the spinal cord?
body.explanation: Transverse diameter 10 to 12 mm, anteroposterior about 8 mm, mass 25 to 30 g.
option_notes: 10 to 12 mm.
Too small.
Too large.
That is the length in cm.

title: What shape is the epiglottic cartilage said to have?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What shape is the epiglottic cartilage said to have?
body.explanation: The epiglottis is shaped like a tennis racket with a curved lower handle forming the foot of the epiglottis. The thyroid is like an open book, the cricoid a signet ring and the arytenoid a triangular pyramid.
option_notes: The signet ring is the cricoid.
The open book is the thyroid.
The pyramid is the arytenoid.
The epiglottis looks like a tennis racket.

title: Why is the cricothyroid called the tuning fork of the larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why is the cricothyroid called the tuning fork of the larynx?
options: It abducts the cords to open the airway
It closes the laryngeal inlet in swallowing
It tenses the cord to vibrate
It relaxes the cords to lower the pitch
body.explanation: The cricothyroid is important for the tone and pitch of the voice: when sound is about to be produced it tenses the vocal cord and makes it ready to vibrate like a tuning fork. Paralysis after an external laryngeal nerve lesion alters the voice significantly, especially in singers.
option_notes: Only the posterior cricoarytenoid abducts.
That is the aryepiglottic sphincter.
It stretches the cord and raises pitch.
It tenses, not relaxes.

title: What is an alternating syndrome?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is an alternating syndrome?
options: Loss of both hearing and balance
body.explanation: A peripheral cranial nerve lesion on one side with hemiplegia on the other locates the lesion to a level in the brainstem.
option_notes: Not this.
Nerve palsy on one side, body weakness on the other.
Not this.
Not this.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
options: Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere
body.explanation: Cerebellar tonsil: the rounded part of the inferior hemisphere beside the vermis, above the foramen magnum.
option_notes: Flocculus is the small lobule beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, part of the flocculonodular lobe.
Posterior lobe of the cerebellar hemisphere is the large part of the cerebellar hemisphere behind the primary fissure.
Vermis is the midline part of the cerebellum joining the two hemispheres.
The rounded part of the inferior hemisphere beside the vermis, above the foramen magnum.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Gyrus rectus (straight gyrus): the straight gyrus on the orbital surface, beside the midline.
option_notes: The straight gyrus on the orbital surface, beside the midline.
Middle frontal gyrus is the middle horizontal gyrus of the lateral frontal lobe.
Fusiform (lateral occipitotemporal) gyrus is the gyrus on the inferior surface between the inferior temporal and parahippocampal gyri.
Cuneus is the wedge of medial occipital cortex between the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci.

title: Which forgotten triangle lies inside the carotid triangle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which forgotten triangle lies inside the carotid triangle?
body.explanation: The carotid triangle contains the triangle of Farabeuf. Lesser's, Pirogoff's and Beclard's triangles are housed within the submandibular triangle.

title: Which layers make up the eyelid, according to the lecture? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which layers make up the eyelid, according to the lecture? (choose all)
body.explanation: The five layers are: skin, loose connective tissue and adipose tissue, the muscular layer (orbicularis oculi and levator palpebrae superioris), the tarsal plate and the palpebral conjunctiva. The sclera and vitreous body belong to the eyeball.

title: Which are actions of parathyroid hormone?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are actions of parathyroid hormone?
body.explanation: Parathyroid secretion participates in the regulation of phosphocalcic metabolism with vitamin D and calcitonin. It is hypercalcemic (increasing bone resorption, promoting intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium) and hypophosphoremic (decreasing renal reabsorption of phosphates).
option_notes: PTH raises calcium.
PTH lowers phosphate.
That is calcitonin.
PTH stimulates bone resorption.

title: What do the longitudinal muscles do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What do the longitudinal muscles do?
options: Constrict the pharynx from above downwards
body.explanation: At the same time the palatopharyngeal sphincter, formed by some fibres of palatopharyngeus, closes the nasopharyngeal isthmus.

title: Which cerebellar peduncle connects the cerebellum to the pons?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cerebellar peduncle connects the cerebellum to the pons?
body.explanation: The superior peduncle joins the midbrain, the middle joins the pons, the inferior joins the medulla.
option_notes: Middle peduncle: pons.
Superior peduncle: midbrain.
Inferior peduncle: medulla.
The cerebral peduncles belong to the midbrain.

title: What does the lumen of the neural tube become?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the lumen of the neural tube become?
body.explanation: The cavity of the neural tube becomes the ventricles and the central canal: the future ventricular system.
option_notes: The ventricles come from the tube's lumen.
That space is outside the brain.
The choroid plexus lies inside the ventricles.
The sinuses are venous channels in the dura.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Inferior colliculus: the lower pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: auditory pathway.
option_notes: The lower pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: auditory pathway.
Midbrain is the top part of the brainstem, between diencephalon and pons.
Cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri) is the thick pillar on the front of the midbrain carrying descending fibres.
Superior colliculus is the upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.

title: Which duct crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which duct crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator?
body.explanation: The main excretory duct, the Stensen's duct, crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator to open at a papilla at the buccal mucosa opposite the maxillary second molar. It measures 4 to 6 mm in length and 5 mm in diameter.

title: Where does the superior cerebellar peduncle send the cerebellum's output?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the superior cerebellar peduncle send the cerebellum's output?
options: To the red nucleus and the thalamus
body.explanation: The superior peduncle is mainly an output pathway to the red nucleus and the thalamus, which projects to the motor cortex.
option_notes: Red nucleus and thalamus.
That is the inferior peduncle's output.
Pontine nuclei send input through the middle peduncle.
The olive sends climbing fibres in.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
options: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
body.explanation: Paracentral lobule: the medial continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri (leg area).
option_notes: Supramarginal gyrus is the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the lateral sulcus.
The medial continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri (leg area).
Transverse temporal gyri (Heschl) is the gyri on the upper surface of the temporal lobe, inside the lateral sulcus: the primary auditory cortex.
Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus is the middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus, part of Broca's area.

title: Where does the larynx extend, superiorly and inferiorly?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the larynx extend, superiorly and inferiorly?
options: From the hyoid bone at C2 to the first tracheal ring at C5
From the base of the tongue at C1 to the thyroid gland at C7
From C4 to the lower edge of C6
From the epiglottis at C3 to the sternal notch at T1
body.explanation: Superior: the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of the body of C4. Inferior: the lower edge of the cricoid cartilage, at the lower edge of C6.
option_notes: The hyoid is above the larynx.
Not these landmarks.
The adult larynx spans about C4 to C6.
Not these landmarks.

title: What is the difference between a chalazion and a stye?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the difference between a chalazion and a stye?
options: A chalazion is infective; a stye is never painful
A chalazion affects the cornea; a stye the retina
A chalazion is in the lid; a stye at its edge
