options: In the bony part of the canal
body.explanation: The thick skin of the cartilaginous part contains hair and ceruminous glands. The thin skin of the bony part has neither.
option_notes: The bony part has thin skin without glands.
They are only in the outer part.
Wax glands and hairs are in the cartilaginous part.
The drum has no glands.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the auricle (pinna). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the cartilage flap outside the head that collects sound.
Not at the arrow; this is air spaces in the mastoid behind the middle ear.
Not at the arrow; this is the three looped canals for balance.
Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the stapes footplate.

title: What is the correct sequence of neural tube formation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the correct sequence of neural tube formation?
options: Neural plate, neural groove, neural tube
Neural tube, neural groove, neural plate
Neural groove, neural plate, neural tube
Neural plate, neural tube, neural groove
body.explanation: Neurulation: ectoderm → neural plate → neural groove → closure of the neural tube.
option_notes: Plate, groove, then tube.
Reversed.
The plate comes first.
The groove comes before the tube.

title: Which structure is NOT part of the brainstem?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is NOT part of the brainstem?
body.explanation: The brainstem is the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata, in descending order. The thalamus belongs to the diencephalon.
option_notes: The thalamus is diencephalon.
Part of the brainstem.
Part of the brainstem.
Part of the brainstem.

title: Which sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes?
body.explanation: The central sulcus of Rolando separates frontal from parietal. The lateral sulcus of Sylvius separates frontal and parietal from temporal.
option_notes: The lateral sulcus is above the temporal lobe.
The central sulcus (Rolando).
The calcarine is in the occipital lobe.
That separates parietal and occipital lobes.

title: Which space lies between the vestibular folds and the vocal folds?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which space lies between the vestibular folds and the vocal folds?
options: The vestibule of the larynx above
body.explanation: Vestibule: the space above the vestibular folds. Ventricle (of Morgagni): between the vestibular folds and the vocal folds. Infraglottic cavity: below the vocal folds.
option_notes: The vestibule lies above the false folds.
The ventricle lies between false and true folds.
The infraglottic cavity lies below the cords.
The piriform recess is in the pharynx.

title: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres? (choose all)
body.explanation: Parasympathetic cranial outflow: III, VII, IX and X.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the vitreous humour. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What does the auditory tube connect?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the auditory tube connect?
options: The middle ear and the pharynx
The nasal cavity and the orbit
The oral cavity and the nose
body.explanation: The auditory (Eustachian, pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the nasopharynx. The torus tubarius is the raised ridge above its opening, and the salpingopharyngeal fold runs down from it.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Thalamus: the large paired grey mass of the diencephalon, the sensory relay.
option_notes: The large paired grey mass of the diencephalon, the sensory relay.
Optic chiasm is where the optic nerves meet and partly cross, in front of the hypothalamus.
Mammillary bodies is the pair of round swellings behind the infundibulum (hypothalamus).
Pineal gland is the small midline gland above the superior colliculi; secretes melatonin.

title: What does the thyroid gland secrete?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the thyroid gland secrete?
body.explanation: The thyroid is a unique median endocrine gland in the neck. It ensures a major metabolic function: the secretion of thyroid hormones and calcitonin.
option_notes: Follicular cells make T3/T4; C cells make calcitonin.
PTH comes from the parathyroids.
These come from the pancreas.
These come from the adrenal cortex.

title: In adults, lumbar puncture is usually done at:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In adults, lumbar puncture is usually done at:
body.explanation: The cord ends at about L1-L2.
option_notes: Below the end of the cord.
Too high; near the cord's end.
Too high.
Too low.

title: Which are well-known landmarks of the neck, according to this paper? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are well-known landmarks of the neck, according to this paper? (choose all)
body.explanation: The paper names the thyroid cartilage, the hyoid bone, the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscle as the well-known landmarks of the neck.

title: What lies in front of the lower anterior wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lies in front of the lower anterior wall?
options: The facial nerve in its canal
body.explanation: The anterior wall separates the cavity from the internal carotid artery below; above it has two openings, for tensor tympani and for the auditory tube.
option_notes: That lies below.
The facial nerve runs on the medial and posterior walls.
The mastoid lies behind.
The internal carotid artery lies in front.

title: What is characteristic of the uveoscleral route?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is characteristic of the uveoscleral route?
options: It is independent of intraocular pressure
It increases sharply with rising intraocular pressure
It drains into the nasolacrimal duct
It is the only route in young people
body.explanation: In the uveoscleral route the aqueous passes from the anterior chamber angle into the connective tissue spaces within the ciliary muscle. Its flow is intraocular pressure independent, so it keeps draining despite pressure fluctuations.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the palpebral conjunctiva. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the thyroid cartilage. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the large shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx (Adam's apple).
Not at the arrow; this is the lateral lobe on the patient's left (viewer's right).
Not at the arrow; this is the lateral lobe on the patient's right (viewer's left).
Not at the arrow; this is the complete ring below the thyroid cartilage.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the hyoid bone. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the U-shaped bone above the larynx.
Not at the arrow; this is the forward bulge where the two thyroid laminae meet.
Not at the arrow; this is the large shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx (Adam's apple).
Not at the arrow; this is the complete ring below the thyroid cartilage.

title: Which gland sits in the sublingual fossa of the mandible?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gland sits in the sublingual fossa of the mandible?
body.explanation: The sublingual fossa lies above the mylohyoid line near the midline and holds the sublingual gland. The submandibular gland sits in the submandibular fossa, below the line.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the loose ct and fat. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which nerve supplies all the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve supplies all the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus?
body.explanation: Motor supply: the hypoglossal nerve supplies all the muscles; the vagus nerve supplies the palatoglossus.

title: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there?
body.explanation: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal: 31 pairs.
option_notes: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
One short.
That is the vertebra count.
Too few.

title: Why does the thyroid move when you swallow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why does the thyroid move when you swallow?
options: Because it is attached to the hyoid by the strap muscles
Because it lies inside the carotid sheath
It is tied to the trachea and larynx
Because the pretracheal fascia is loose
body.explanation: The posteromedial border of the lateral lobe is attached to the first three tracheal rings by the thyro-tracheal ligament. The thyroid body is united with the trachea and larynx, so it follows their movement during swallowing.
option_notes: The strap muscles are not the reason.
It is not in the carotid sheath.
Its fascia and Berry's ligament tie it to the larynx and trachea.
Not the reason.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the optic tract. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structures bound Farabeuf's triangle? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures bound Farabeuf's triangle? (choose all)
body.explanation: Farabeuf's triangle is bounded by the internal jugular vein posteriorly, the common facial vein anteroinferiorly and the hypoglossal nerve superiorly.

title: What is the main role of the cerebellum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the main role of the cerebellum?
options: Automatic regulation of movement: tone, balance and coordination
Relaying all sensations to the cortex
body.explanation: The cerebellum regulates motor activity automatically: muscle tone, balance and coordination of voluntary movements.
option_notes: It corrects and coordinates movement.
The motor cortex starts voluntary movements.
The thalamus relays sensation.
The choroid plexus makes CSF.

title: Where is Wernicke's area?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is Wernicke's area?
body.explanation: Wernicke's area, for understanding language, lies in the posterior superior temporal lobe, at the end of the first temporal sulcus, linked to Broca's area.
option_notes: Back of the superior temporal gyrus.
That is Broca's area.
That is visual.
That is motor.

title: Which face of the lateral lobe is applied to the trachea and larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which face of the lateral lobe is applied to the trachea and larynx?
body.explanation: Three sides: a peripheral (anterolateral) convex superficial face; a medial (internal) visceral side applied to the lateral side of the trachea and the lower larynx; and a posterior face moulded on the vascular-nervous bundle of the neck.
option_notes: The anterolateral face is covered by the strap muscles.
The posterior face faces the carotid sheath.
The medial face lies on the larynx and trachea.
Not a named face here.

title: Which of these is NOT a stated function of the nose?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which of these is NOT a stated function of the nose?
body.explanation: The six functions given are respiration, olfaction, protection of the lower respiratory passages, air conditioning of the inspired air, vocal resonance, and nasal reflex functions such as sneezing.

title: Which four projections of the lateral auricle are constant?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which four projections of the lateral auricle are constant?
body.explanation: The helix runs around the upper two thirds; the anthelix is a bifid projection concentric to it, separated by the scapha; then the tragus and antitragus.
option_notes: The concha is a hollow, and the lobe and scapha are not counted as the constant projections.
The concha and cymba are hollows.
The lobe, scapha and concha are not projections.
Helix, anthelix, tragus and antitragus are the four constant projections.

title: Which functions does the larynx perform?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functions does the larynx perform?
body.explanation: The functions of the larynx are phonation, respiration, protection and deglutition. It acts as a sphincter at the inlet of the lower respiratory tract.
option_notes: The larynx produces voice.
It closes to protect the airway.
Smell is the nose.
Chewing is the jaw.

title: Which branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the structures of the upper larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which branch of the superior thyroid artery supplies the structures of the upper larynx?
options: Cricothyroid branch of the same artery
body.explanation: The superior thyroid artery divides into four branches: infrahyoid (infrahyoid muscles), superior laryngeal (upper larynx), cricothyroid (cricothyroid muscle) and glandular (superior aspect of the thyroid).

title: Which muscle abducts the eyeball and takes the abducens nerve?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle abducts the eyeball and takes the abducens nerve?
body.explanation: The lateral rectus arises from the common ring tendon, inserts on the anterior and lateral surface, and abducts the eyeball. It is the only muscle supplied by CN VI.

title: Which functional area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functional area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: The precentral gyrus, in front of the central sulcus, is the primary motor cortex (motor strip).
option_notes: Primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus.
Primary motor cortex lies in the precentral gyrus.
Primary visual cortex lies in the banks of the calcarine sulcus.
Primary auditory cortex lies in the transverse temporal gyri (Heschl).

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the posterior semicircular canal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the vertical canal facing backward.
Not at the arrow; this is the vertical canal at the top, facing forward.
Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
Not at the arrow; this is the bony core the cochlea winds around.

title: Which artery mainly supplies the brainstem?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery mainly supplies the brainstem?
body.explanation: Branches include the posterior cerebral artery and its peduncular branch, the superior cerebellar artery, the posterior choroidal artery and the interpeduncular branches.
option_notes: Anterior circulation.
Anterior circulation.
Only part.
The vertebrobasilar system.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
options: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus
body.explanation: Precuneus: the medial parietal area in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
option_notes: Triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus is the middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus, part of Broca's area.
Lingual gyrus is the medial occipital gyrus below the calcarine sulcus.
Temporal pole is the front tip of the temporal lobe.
The medial parietal area in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.

title: What lies between the bony and membranous labyrinths?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lies between the bony and membranous labyrinths?
body.explanation: The membranous labyrinth lies within the bony labyrinth in the petrous temporal bone, and the space between them is filled with perilymph.
option_notes: Endolymph is inside the membranous labyrinth.
Perilymph fills the space between the two labyrinths.
Air is in the middle ear.
Not blood.

title: Which nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression?
body.explanation: All the muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve. The trigeminal nerve, through V3, supplies the muscles of mastication instead.

title: What is the Greek word for nose, giving the name of the specialty?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the Greek word for nose, giving the name of the specialty?
body.explanation: The Greek word for nose is rhinos, so the study of the nose and its diseases is termed rhinology.

title: Which are ascending (sensory) tracts?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are ascending (sensory) tracts?
body.explanation: Ascending: dorsal columns and spinothalamic tracts. Descending: corticospinal and vestibulospinal.
option_notes: Ascending.
Ascending.
Descending.
Descending.

title: Which retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which retinal fibres cross at the optic chiasm?
body.explanation: Fibres from the medial (nasal) half of each retina cross over to the optic tract of the opposite side. The temporal fibres stay on the same side.

title: What movement happens at the cricothyroid joint?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What movement happens at the cricothyroid joint?
options: Rotation of the arytenoid around a vertical axis
Gliding of one arytenoid toward the other
body.explanation: The cricothyroid joint is a flat synovial joint between the lower cornu of the thyroid cartilage and the lateral face of the cricoid. Tilting of the arch up and the lamina down tenses the vocal cords.
option_notes: That is the cricoarytenoid joint.
That is the cricoarytenoid joint.
Extrinsic muscles do this.
The cricoid tilts on the thyroid, lengthening the cords.

title: Roughly how many rods and cones does the retina contain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Roughly how many rods and cones does the retina contain?
options: About 6 million rods and 120 million cones
About 120 million rods and 6 million cones
body.explanation: The retina has approximately 120 million rods, extremely sensitive to light, and 6 million cones in each retina.

title: Who was Farabeuf's triangle named after?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Who was Farabeuf's triangle named after?
options: A German surgeon, Ladislaus Leon Lesser
A French surgeon, Louis Hubert Farabeuf
body.explanation: Farabeuf's triangle is named after the French surgeon Louis Hubert Farabeuf, who lived from 1841 to 1910.

title: The total volume of CSF in an adult is about:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The total volume of CSF in an adult is about:
body.explanation: About 125 mL subarachnoid and 25 mL ventricular; about 500 mL is made each day.
option_notes: Too little.
About 150 mL.
That is daily production.
Far too much.

title: Which structures make up the membranous labyrinth?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures make up the membranous labyrinth?
body.explanation: Membranous: semicircular ducts, cochlear duct, utricle, saccule. The modiolus and the vestibule are bony.
option_notes: The utricle is membranous.
The cochlear duct is membranous.
The modiolus is bone.
The vestibule is bony.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Third ventricle. Median cleft between the two thalami, in the diencephalon.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the openings from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle.
Not at the arrow; this is the venous sinus along the top of the falx, where CSF drains.
Not at the arrow; this is the tufts pushing into the sinus that absorb CSF.
This is at the arrow: the narrow midline cavity between the two thalami.

title: Which muscle inserts into the superior tarsus and the skin of the upper eyelid?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle inserts into the superior tarsus and the skin of the upper eyelid?
body.explanation: It arises from the lesser wing of the sphenoid, superior and anterior to the optic canal. Its deep layer, the superior tarsal muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres. Its action is elevating the upper eyelid.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the sphenoid sinus. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the superior thyroid. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which sensation is NOT filtered by the thalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which sensation is NOT filtered by the thalamus?
body.explanation: Your professor's question. Olfactory inputs exist but are not filtered; all other sensations are processed in the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
option_notes: Smell reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.
Passes through the thalamus.
Passes through the thalamus.
Passes through the thalamus.

title: Which hair cells carry most auditory information to the brain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which hair cells carry most auditory information to the brain?
body.explanation: Inner hair cells ensure mechano-electrical transduction and connect to about 45,000 afferent fibres, 90 to 95 percent of the cochlear nerve. Outer hair cells are contractile and innervated by efferent fibres, increasing frequency selectivity.
option_notes: Inner hair cells send most afferent fibres.
Outer hair cells mainly amplify.
Supporting cells are not receptors.
Rods are in the retina.

title: Which muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III)? (choose all)
body.explanation: CN III supplies the levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus and inferior oblique. The superior oblique is CN IV and the lateral rectus is CN VI.

title: What is the most common cause of sciatica?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the most common cause of sciatica?
body.explanation: The most common cause of sciatica is a bulging or herniated intervertebral disc compressing the nerve roots.

title: What forms the posterior boundary of the subthalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the posterior boundary of the subthalamus?
options: The red nucleus and substantia nigra
body.explanation: Subthalamus boundaries: hypothalamus medially, internal capsule laterally, red nucleus and substantia nigra posteriorly.
option_notes: Posterior boundary.
Lateral boundary.
Medial boundary.
Not a boundary of the subthalamus.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the cerebral peduncle (midbrain). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which is the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords?
body.explanation: All the intrinsic muscles adduct the vocal cords except the posterior cricoarytenoids, which abduct them. They are called the safety muscles of the larynx: if they are paralysed the adductors take the upper hand and the person may die from lack of air.
option_notes: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor.
It adducts.
It adducts.
It tenses.

title: Which muscle is described as the pouting muscle of the chin?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle is described as the pouting muscle of the chin?
body.explanation: The mentalis arises from the mandible below the incisor teeth and inserts into the skin of the chin. It raises and protrudes the lower lip, wrinkling the chin skin.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the orbit. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Putamen: the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.
option_notes: Amygdala is the almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, at the tip of the temporal horn: emotion.
The outer part of the lentiform nucleus.
Globus pallidus is the inner part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen.
Fornix is the arched fibre tract from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.

title: In most people, which hemisphere is dominant for language?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In most people, which hemisphere is dominant for language?
body.explanation: The left hemisphere controls speech, comprehension, arithmetic and writing; the right creativity, spatial, artistic and musical skills.
option_notes: Right is dominant in a minority.
Not equal.
Too low.
The left in about 92%.

title: A patient develops violent, flinging movements of the right arm after a small stroke. Which structure is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A patient develops violent, flinging movements of the right arm after a small stroke. Which structure is damaged?
body.explanation: Lesions of the subthalamic nucleus cause hemiballismus on the opposite side of the body.
option_notes: Hemiballismus appears on the side opposite the lesion.
A right lesion would affect the left side.
The LGB is visual.
The pineal does not cause abnormal movements.

title: Which structures pass through the foramina of the cribriform plate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures pass through the foramina of the cribriform plate?
body.explanation: The cribriform plate is the sieve-like roof of the nasal cavity. Its small openings carry the fibres of the olfactory nerves from the nose to the brain.

title: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
body.explanation: Four nerves emerge from the medulla: IX, X and the cranial part of XI behind the olive, and XII between pyramid and olive.
option_notes: IX emerges behind the olive.
X emerges behind the olive.
XII emerges between pyramid and olive.
III emerges from the midbrain.

title: Which reflex is monosynaptic?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which reflex is monosynaptic?
body.explanation: The knee jerk: quadriceps stretch activates the muscle spindle, the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron, and the muscle contracts. It tests spinal segment integrity.

title: Which are signs of Horner's syndrome? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are signs of Horner's syndrome? (choose all)
body.explanation: A lesion of the sympathetic pathway causes ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

title: Which turbinate is inconstant?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which turbinate is inconstant?
body.explanation: There are three, sometimes four, conchae. The supreme turbinate is inconstant.

title: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Fourth ventricle: the ventricle between the brainstem and cerebellum.
option_notes: Choroid plexus is the vascular tufts in the ventricles that produce CSF.
Cerebral aqueduct is the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.
The ventricle between the brainstem and cerebellum.
Lateral ventricle is the C-shaped ventricle in each hemisphere.

title: Where is lymphatic drainage of the larynx absent?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is lymphatic drainage of the larynx absent?
body.explanation: Lymphatic drainage is very rich in the supraglottic zone, thinner in the subglottic zone and absent at the vocal cords. Supraglottic drains to the internal jugular chain; infraglottic to the pretracheal and paratracheal nodes and the internal jugular chain.
option_notes: The vocal cords have almost no lymphatics.
Rich drainage.
Has drainage.
Has drainage.

title: Which tracheal rings does the posterior aspect of the isthmus cover?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which tracheal rings does the posterior aspect of the isthmus cover?
body.explanation: The posterior aspect of the thyroid isthmus covers the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings, and is attached to the trachea by the thyro-tracheal ligament, the median ligament of Berry.
option_notes: Too high.
Too low.
Too low.
The isthmus covers tracheal rings 2 to 4.

title: Where does the oculomotor nerve emerge?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the oculomotor nerve emerge?
body.explanation: CN III exits between the peduncles, in the interpeduncular fossa, while the optic tract runs around the upper border of the midbrain.
option_notes: That is VI.
That is IX to XI.
III leaves in the interpeduncular fossa.
IV leaves behind.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Hypothalamus: the region below the thalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle.
option_notes: The region below the thalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle.
Thalamus is the large paired grey mass on either side of the third ventricle.
Putamen is the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.
Caudate nucleus is the C-shaped nucleus curving along the lateral ventricle.

title: What forms the posterolateral boundary of the posterior triangle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What forms the posterolateral boundary of the posterior triangle?
body.explanation: The posterior triangle is bounded anteromedially by the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, posterolaterally by the anterior border of trapezius, and inferiorly by the clavicle.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the vestibule. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the central chamber of the bony labyrinth, between cochlea and canals.
Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
Not at the arrow; this is the swelling at one end of each canal, holding the crista.
Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the stapes footplate.

title: Which branch of the ophthalmic artery supplies the retina?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which branch of the ophthalmic artery supplies the retina?
options: The frontal artery of the orbit
body.explanation: The central retinal artery branches off the posterior third of the ophthalmic artery and enters the dural sheath of the optic nerve about 13 mm behind the globe. It supplies the retina.

title: Which veins drain the nasal cavity? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which veins drain the nasal cavity? (choose all)
body.explanation: Venous drainage has two networks, a deep periosteal and a superficial mucous one, draining to the internal maxillary vein, the ophthalmic vein and the facial vein.

title: Which muscle forms the muscular component of the cheek?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle forms the muscular component of the cheek?
body.explanation: The buccinator is a thin quadrilateral muscle between the maxilla and mandible. It compresses the cheeks so food stays between the teeth during chewing, and it is used in blowing and suckling.

title: Which two muscles intort the eyeball?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which two muscles intort the eyeball?
body.explanation: Intorsion is done by the two superior muscles, superior oblique and superior rectus; extorsion by the two inferior muscles, inferior oblique and inferior rectus.

title: What is the pulvinar?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the pulvinar?
options: A part of the pineal gland
body.explanation: The pulvinar is the posterior nuclear group, the rearmost part of the thalamus, lateral to the pineal gland.
option_notes: The anterior part is the anterior nucleus.
The pulvinar is the posterior thalamus.
Not hypothalamic.
Not pineal.

title: What separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
body.explanation: The falx cerebri, a crescent-shaped fold of dura, incompletely separates the hemispheres. The tentorium cerebelli separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum.
option_notes: The tentorium separates cerebrum from cerebellum.
The falx cerebri lies in the longitudinal fissure.
Bichat's fissure is a transverse slit.
The corpus callosum joins them.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Precentral gyrus: the gyrus just in front of the central sulcus: the primary motor cortex.
option_notes: Inferior temporal gyrus is the lowest gyrus of the lateral temporal lobe.
The gyrus just in front of the central sulcus: the primary motor cortex.
Parahippocampal gyrus is the medial temporal gyrus on the inferior surface, ending in front in the uncus.
Precuneus is the medial parietal area in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.

title: Choroid plexus is normally absent from:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Choroid plexus is normally absent from:
options: The body of the lateral ventricle
body.explanation: Also absent from the frontal and occipital horns.
option_notes: Present.
The aqueduct has no choroid plexus.
Present.
Present.

title: Which sinuses drain into the middle meatus? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which sinuses drain into the middle meatus? (choose all)
body.explanation: Middle meatus: the maxillary sinus (via the ethmoidal infundibulum), the frontal sinus (via the frontonasal duct) and the anterior and middle ethmoidal cells. The sphenoidal sinus opens into the spheno-ethmoidal recess; the posterior ethmoidal cells into the superior meatus.

title: Which division of the autonomic system prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which division of the autonomic system prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
body.explanation: Sympathetic: fight or flight. Parasympathetic: rest and digest.
option_notes: Sympathetic: fight or flight.
Parasympathetic: rest and digest.
Somatic is voluntary, not autonomic.
Not the division named in the lecture.

title: What happens if one recurrent laryngeal nerve is damaged?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What happens if one recurrent laryngeal nerve is damaged?
options: Both cords become fixed in abduction
Only sensation above the cords is lost
body.explanation: Unilateral damage leaves the cord on the affected side in the paramedian position, between abduction and adduction, not vibrating. Usually the other cord compensates and phonation is not much affected.
option_notes: That is bilateral palsy.
The other cord compensates.
The paralysed cord sits near the midline (paramedian).
That is the internal branch.

title: What is Tenon's capsule?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is Tenon's capsule?
options: The fascial sheath of the eyeball
The outermost vascular layer of the sclera
The mucous membrane lining the eyelid
The jelly filling the posterior segment
body.explanation: Tenon's capsule, the fascial sheath of the eyeball, separates the eye from the orbital fat and forms a socket in which it moves.

title: What determines the size of a body part's motor area?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What determines the size of a body part's motor area?
body.explanation: Cortical extent follows the complexity and precision of movement, not muscle size, so the hand and tongue areas are the largest.

title: How many cartilages does the larynx have?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many cartilages does the larynx have?
body.explanation: Nine cartilages: three unpaired (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis) and three paired (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform). The principal ones are the cricoid, the thyroid and the two arytenoids.
option_notes: Three unpaired and three paired: nine in total.
Six counts each type once; the paired ones count twice.
Too few.
Too many.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Optic chiasm: where the optic nerves meet and partly cross, in front of the hypothalamus.
option_notes: Where the optic nerves meet and partly cross, in front of the hypothalamus.
Mammillary bodies is the pair of round swellings behind the infundibulum (hypothalamus).
Lateral geniculate body is the thalamic relay for vision.
Pineal gland is the small midline gland above the superior colliculi; secretes melatonin.

title: The medial wall of the frontal horn is formed by:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The medial wall of the frontal horn is formed by:
options: The head of the caudate nucleus
body.explanation: The head of the caudate forms the lateral wall.
option_notes: The tapetum lines the temporal and occipital horns.
Forms the lateral wall.
Lines the body.
The septum pellucidum forms the medial wall.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Flocculus: the small lobule beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, part of the flocculonodular lobe.
option_notes: The small lobule beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, part of the flocculonodular lobe.
Vermis is the midline part of the cerebellum joining the two hemispheres.
Superior cerebellar peduncle is the bundle joining the cerebellum to the midbrain; the main cerebellar output.
Anterior lobe of the cerebellum is the smaller part of the cerebellar hemisphere in front of the primary fissure.

title: Damage to the optic tract or the fibre tract from the lateral geniculate to the cortex causes what?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Damage to the optic tract or the fibre tract from the lateral geniculate to the cortex causes what?
options: A defect only in the damaged eye
body.explanation: Damage at sites 4 and 5 causes identical visual loss: in the lecture's example, loss of vision of the right side.

title: According to the lecture, which neurotransmitters are excitatory in the basal ganglia? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: According to the lecture, which neurotransmitters are excitatory in the basal ganglia? (choose all)
body.explanation: Acetylcholine (cholinergic interneurons of the striatum) and glutamate (subthalamic and cortical afferents) excite. GABA inhibits, and the lecture presents dopamine as the main inhibitory transmitter of the extrapyramidal system.
option_notes: Excitatory: produced by cholinergic interneurons of the striatum (slide 52).
Excitatory: used by cortical and subthalamic projections.
Inhibitory: the main output transmitter of striatum and pallidum.
The lecture calls dopamine the main inhibitory transmitter of the extrapyramidal system (slide 51).

title: Which muscles do the vestibulospinal tracts activate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles do the vestibulospinal tracts activate?
body.explanation: They carry balance information from the vestibular nuclei, ipsilaterally, to anti-gravity muscles: flexors of the arm and extensors of the leg.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the oropharynx. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: The cerebral aqueduct connects:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The cerebral aqueduct connects:
options: The lateral ventricles and the third ventricle
The fourth ventricle and the subarachnoid space
The lateral ventricle and the subarachnoid space
body.explanation: It runs through the midbrain.
option_notes: That is Monro.
That is Luschka and Magendie.
It joins the third and fourth ventricles.
Not a direct connection.

title: What is Little's area, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is Little's area, and why does it matter?
options: A vascular area of the anterior septum
The olfactory area of the superior septum
The opening of the maxillary sinus
body.explanation: Little's area lies in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule. The septal branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose there to form Kiesselbach's plexus. It is the commonest site of nose bleeding in children and young adults, usually from fingernail trauma.

title: Where is the trigeminal ganglion?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the trigeminal ganglion?
body.explanation: The sensory fibres synapse in the large trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion in Meckel's cave.

title: Name the three constrictor muscles.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the three constrictor muscles.
body.explanation: The pharyngeal muscles are the three constrictors (superior, middle, inferior) and three elevators (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus).

title: Which embryonic zone of the neural tube becomes the white matter?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which embryonic zone of the neural tube becomes the white matter?
body.explanation: The marginal zone, outermost and containing nerve fibres, becomes white matter.
option_notes: Outermost: white matter.
Becomes grey matter.
Gives neuroblasts and glioblasts, then the ependyma.
Part of the mantle; sensory neurons.

title: Which structure alters the shape and thickness of the lens?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure alters the shape and thickness of the lens?
body.explanation: The ciliary body is a muscular structure connecting the choroid with the circumference of the iris. It alters the shape and thickness of the lens (accommodation), and its ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour.

title: Which cortical layer contains the Betz cells?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cortical layer contains the Betz cells?
body.explanation: The motor cortex has six layers. Layer IV, well developed in the parietal cortex, is almost absent in the motor cortex. Layer V holds the large Betz cells, the origin of the pyramidal tract.

title: Which lobes are separated by the lateral sulcus (Sylvius)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which lobes are separated by the lateral sulcus (Sylvius)?
options: The temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above
The frontal lobe from the parietal lobe
The parietal lobe from the occipital lobe
body.explanation: The lateral sulcus separates the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe.
option_notes: The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus.
That is the central sulcus.
That is the parieto-occipital sulcus.
That is the longitudinal fissure, with the falx.

title: The zygomatic arch is formed by the temporal process of the zygomatic bone and which other structure?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The zygomatic arch is formed by the temporal process of the zygomatic bone and which other structure?
options: Frontal process of the zygomatic bone
Zygomatic process of the frontal bone
body.explanation: The arch is completed by the zygomatic process of the temporal bone joining the temporal process of the zygomatic bone at the temporozygomatic suture.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the lateral sulcus (sylvius). The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the gyrus behind the central sulcus.
This is at the arrow: the deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
Not at the arrow; this is the inferior frontal gyrus, usually on the left.
Not at the arrow; this is the lobe at the back of the hemisphere.

title: Which disorders are linked to epithalamic dysfunction?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which disorders are linked to epithalamic dysfunction?
body.explanation: Dysfunction of the epithalamus is linked to major depression, schizophrenia and sleep disorders; low melatonin tends to cause mood disorders.
option_notes: Basal ganglia.
Melatonin and the habenula link it to mood and sleep.
Visual pathway.
Not linked.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the uvula. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Supramarginal gyrus: the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the lateral sulcus.
option_notes: Postcentral gyrus is the gyrus just behind the central sulcus: the primary somatosensory cortex.
Lingual gyrus is the medial occipital gyrus below the calcarine sulcus.
The parietal gyrus arching around the end of the lateral sulcus.
Cingulate gyrus is the gyrus arching around the corpus callosum on the medial surface (limbic lobe).

title: Which structure separates the brainstem from the diencephalon above?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure separates the brainstem from the diencephalon above?
body.explanation: The brainstem connects above to the diencephalon at the transverse fissure of Bichat, and below to the cord at the foramen magnum.
option_notes: Upper limit.
Lower limit.
Between pons and medulla.
Side landmark.

title: Where does the sciatic nerve usually divide?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the sciatic nerve usually divide?
body.explanation: It descends in the posterior thigh on adductor magnus, supplying the hamstrings, and divides near the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

title: Where do the dorsal (sensory) roots come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do the dorsal (sensory) roots come from?
body.explanation: Ventral motor roots arise from basal plate motor neurons; dorsal sensory roots arise from neural crest cells outside the neural tube.
option_notes: Motor.
Not the source.
No.
Dorsal root ganglia come from the neural crest.

title: Which processes does the inferior concha have?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which processes does the inferior concha have?
body.explanation: The inferior turbinate has three processes: lacrimal, ethmoidal and maxillary. Its medial side faces the septum and its lateral side the inferior meatus.

title: What sits in the tectum of the midbrain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What sits in the tectum of the midbrain?
body.explanation: The tectum, behind the cerebral aqueduct, houses two superior and two inferior colliculi, just below the pineal gland.
option_notes: Medulla.
Medulla.
Superior and inferior colliculi.
Floor of the fourth ventricle.

title: Which is the smallest ossicle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the smallest ossicle?
body.explanation: The stapes is the smallest and lightest, about 2 mg, with a head, anterior and posterior crura and a footplate.
option_notes: The malleus is the largest.
The incus is middle-sized.
The stapes is the smallest bone in the body.
Sizes differ.

title: Which are features of scotopic vision? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which are features of scotopic vision? (choose all)
body.explanation: Scotopic: night and dim light vision, served by rods, low visual acuity, no colours or details, great sensitivity to light. Photopic vision by cones gives colour and detail.

title: What fills the membranous labyrinth?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What fills the membranous labyrinth?
body.explanation: The membranous labyrinth is a closed system of fluid-filled sacs and ducts containing endolymph. The space between it and the bony labyrinth holds perilymph.
option_notes: The membranous labyrinth is filled with endolymph.
Perilymph surrounds it.
CSF is around the brain; perilymph only connects with it.
The inner ear holds fluid, not air.

title: Where is the inferior parathyroid gland found?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where is the inferior parathyroid gland found?
options: Inside the true capsule of the thyroid
body.explanation: The inferior parathyroid lies on the posteromedial border of the lateral lobe, outside the inferior laryngeal nerve, below the termination of the inferior thyroid artery. The superior parathyroid lies on the same posteromedial border.
option_notes: Not in front.
On the posterior border, near the lower pole.
They lie outside the true capsule.
Not in the carotid sheath.

title: Which muscle lies on the outer aspect of the larynx?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscle lies on the outer aspect of the larynx?
body.explanation: The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic muscle lying on the outer aspect of the larynx. That is also why it is reached by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
option_notes: The vocalis is inside the cord.
Internal.
Internal.
The cricothyroid is on the outside of the larynx.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the anterior (superior) semicircular canal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the opening closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
Not at the arrow; this is the central chamber of the bony labyrinth, between cochlea and canals.
Not at the arrow; this is the vertical canal facing backward.
This is at the arrow: the vertical canal at the top, facing forward.

title: In facial nerve palsy, what happens to the eye?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In facial nerve palsy, what happens to the eye?
options: The pupil becomes fixed and dilated
Vision is lost in that eye
body.explanation: In facial nerve palsy the person cannot wrinkle the brow, the eyelid droops and the eye is difficult to close completely, the smile is asymmetrical, and the corner of the mouth droops.

title: What is the ethmoid bulla?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the ethmoid bulla?
options: A bony spur of the nasal septum
The opening of the maxillary sinus
A thickening of the inferior concha
A swelling of the meatus wall
body.explanation: The thin-walled, bony, honeycombed spaces collectively form the ethmoidal labyrinth, located between the orbits and the nasal fossae. The ethmoid bulla is produced by the middle ethmoid air cells and swells the lateral wall of the middle meatus.

title: Which three acoustic parameters characterise the voice?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which three acoustic parameters characterise the voice?
body.explanation: Frequency, in Hertz, depends on the vibration speed of the vocal folds. Intensity, in dB, depends on the force of pulmonary expiration (subglottic pressure). Pitch depends on the accommodation of the vocal folds but especially on the shape of the supralaryngeal cavities.
option_notes: Not these.
Frequency, intensity and pitch.
Not these.
Not these.

title: Why is a lumbar puncture done below the second lumbar vertebra in adults?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why is a lumbar puncture done below the second lumbar vertebra in adults?
options: The spinal cord ends around L1-L2, so the needle meets only nerve roots and CSF
CSF is only found below L2
body.explanation: The cord ends around L1-L2 but the lumbar subarachnoid space extends below it, so puncture is done at L3-L4 or L4-L5.
option_notes: This avoids injuring the cord.
CSF surrounds the whole cord.
The dural sac continues to about S2.
Not the reason.

title: Which two nuclei form the lentiform nucleus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which two nuclei form the lentiform nucleus?
body.explanation: Putamen plus globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus; caudate plus putamen form the dorsal striatum.
option_notes: Caudate plus putamen is the striatum.
Putamen plus globus pallidus.
Not the lentiform.
Not the lentiform.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Amygdala: the almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, at the tip of the temporal horn: emotion.
option_notes: Hippocampus is the curved structure in the floor of the temporal horn: memory.
The almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, at the tip of the temporal horn: emotion.
Globus pallidus is the inner part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen.
Putamen is the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.

title: What are the four ventilatory functions of the nose?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the four ventilatory functions of the nose?
body.explanation: The ventilatory function has four parts: airflow control (rheostat), filtration, humidification (hygrostat) and heating (thermostat).

title: Which structures belong to the peripheral nervous system?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures belong to the peripheral nervous system?
body.explanation: The PNS is all neural elements outside the CNS: cranial nerves, spinal nerves and peripheral ganglia.
option_notes: 12 pairs, part of the PNS.
31 pairs, part of the PNS.
Sensory ganglia are PNS.
The spinal cord is CNS.

title: What shape is the pharynx, and what is it made of?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What shape is the pharynx, and what is it made of?
body.explanation: The pharynx is a funnel-shaped fibromuscular tube extending from the base of the skull to the oesophagus, lined throughout with mucous membrane.

title: In a dislocation of the temporomandibular joint, the head of the mandible slips out of the mandibular fossa and is pulled in which direction?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In a dislocation of the temporomandibular joint, the head of the mandible slips out of the mandibular fossa and is pulled in which direction?
body.explanation: The head slips out and is pulled forward, so the patient cannot close the mouth. A blow to the side of the face, yawning or a large bite can cause it.

title: Which part of the auricle has no cartilage framework?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the auricle has no cartilage framework?
body.explanation: The ear lobe is a simple skin fold without a cartilage framework.
option_notes: The helix has a cartilage frame.
The lobule is just skin and fat, with no cartilage.
The anthelix has a cartilage frame.
The tragus has a cartilage frame.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Superior colliculus: the upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.
option_notes: Midbrain is the top part of the brainstem, between diencephalon and pons.
Pons is the bulging middle part of the brainstem.
The upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: visual reflexes.
Cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri) is the thick pillar on the front of the midbrain carrying descending fibres.

title: What effect do the sympathetic fibres have on the lacrimal gland?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What effect do the sympathetic fibres have on the lacrimal gland?
options: They have no effect on the gland
body.explanation: Parasympathetic fibres stimulate fluid secretion from the lacrimal gland. Sympathetic fibres, from the superior cervical ganglion travelling on the internal carotid plexus and the deep petrosal nerve, inhibit it.

title: Where does lymph from the lacrimal gland drain?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does lymph from the lacrimal gland drain?
body.explanation: Lymphatic drainage is to the superficial parotid lymph nodes, which empty into the superior deep cervical nodes.

title: Where does the inferior thyroid artery come from?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where does the inferior thyroid artery come from?
body.explanation: The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, a collateral of the subclavian artery. It divides into a posterior, an inferior and a middle branch.
option_notes: That gives the superior artery.
Not usually.
The thyrocervical trunk (subclavian).
Not directly.

title: Which part of the retina is responsible for high-acuity vision?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the retina is responsible for high-acuity vision?
options: The fovea, at the centre of the macula
The optic disc, where the nerve leaves
body.explanation: The macula contains special photoreceptor cones for visual acuity and lacks blood vessels. At its centre is the fovea, responsible for high-acuity vision and densely saturated with cone photoreceptors.

title: Which structure forms the posterior part of the hard palate?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure forms the posterior part of the hard palate?
body.explanation: The palatine processes of the maxillae form the front of the hard palate, and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones complete it behind.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Globus pallidus: the inner part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen.
option_notes: Caudate nucleus is the C-shaped nucleus curving along the lateral ventricle.
Amygdala is the almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, at the tip of the temporal horn: emotion.
The inner part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen.
Putamen is the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Hippocampus: the curved structure in the floor of the temporal horn: memory.
option_notes: Globus pallidus is the inner part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen.
Amygdala is the almond-shaped nucleus in front of the hippocampus, at the tip of the temporal horn: emotion.
Fornix is the arched fibre tract from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies.
The curved structure in the floor of the temporal horn: memory.

title: Which lobe is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which lobe is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Occipital lobe: at the back, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus.
option_notes: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus, in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
The frontal lobe lies in front of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus.
The temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus.
The occipital lobe lies at the back, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus.

title: Which muscles belong to the muscles of mastication? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which muscles belong to the muscles of mastication? (choose all)
body.explanation: The four muscles of mastication are the temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid. The buccinator and platysma are muscles of facial expression, supplied by CN VII.

title: Why is the corticobulbar tract also called the geniculate tract?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Why is the corticobulbar tract also called the geniculate tract?
options: It starts in the geniculate ganglion
body.explanation: The corticonuclear or geniculate pathway links the motor cortex to the cranial nerve nuclei and passes through the genu of the internal capsule.

title: Which structures belong to the vascular layer (uvea)? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures belong to the vascular layer (uvea)? (choose all)
body.explanation: The uvea is made of the iris, the ciliary body and the choroid. The sclera belongs to the fibrous layer and the retina to the neural layer.

title: Which structures are on the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex? (choose all)
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structures are on the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex? (choose all)
body.explanation: Efferent: Edinger-Westphal nucleus, oculomotor nerve, ciliary ganglion, short ciliary nerves, sphincter pupillae. The optic nerve and the lateral geniculate nucleus belong to the afferent side and to vision.

title: The external jugular vein drains into which vein?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The external jugular vein drains into which vein?
body.explanation: The external jugular vein descends over the sternocleidomastoid, beneath the platysma, and drains into the subclavian vein behind the middle of the clavicle.

title: In myopia (nearsightedness), where does the image focus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: In myopia (nearsightedness), where does the image focus?
options: Exactly on the fovea, in focus
body.explanation: A nearsighted person sees near objects clearly while distant objects are blurred. Farsightedness (hyperopia) is the image being focused behind the retina rather than directly on it, which may be caused by the eyeball being too small or the focusing power being too weak.

title: A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere most typically causes which finding?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: A lesion of the right cerebellar hemisphere most typically causes which finding?
body.explanation: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body, so signs are ipsilateral.
option_notes: Cerebellar signs are on the same side.
That would be the left hemisphere.
The cerebellum causes incoordination, not paralysis.
Pain is carried by the spinothalamic tract.

title: What is the optic disc, and why is it called the blind spot?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the optic disc, and why is it called the blind spot?
options: The area of highest cone density, which lacks rods
A defect in the iris that blocks light
Where the optic nerve leaves: no photoreceptors
The point where the retina meets the ora serrata
body.explanation: The optic disc (papilla) is located in the fundus of the retina, where the sensory fibres of the optic nerve enter the eyeball. It has no photoreceptors, hence the blind spot.

title: Which nerve supplies the buccinator and orbicularis oris?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which nerve supplies the buccinator and orbicularis oris?
body.explanation: Motor supply: the muscle in the cheek (buccinator) and the lip (orbicularis oris) are supplied by branches of the facial nerve.

title: Which is the main relay station for sensory pathways on their way to the cortex (except smell)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which is the main relay station for sensory pathways on their way to the cortex (except smell)?
body.explanation: All sensory stimuli except smell are processed in the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
option_notes: The thalamus relays all senses except smell.
The hypothalamus controls homeostasis and hormones.
The hippocampus is for memory.
The amygdala is for emotion.

title: Which orbital wall is most prone to blowout fracture?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which orbital wall is most prone to blowout fracture?
body.explanation: The most common blowout fractures are those of the inferior orbital wall, the floor. In about half of cases they occur together with fractures of the medial orbital wall.

title: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerve is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Hypoglossal nerve (XII): leaves the medulla between the pyramid and the olive.
option_notes: Leaves the medulla between the pyramid and the olive.
Abducens nerve (VI) is leaves at the pontomedullary junction, near the midline.
Vagus nerve (X) is leaves the medulla behind the olive, below IX.
Oculomotor nerve (III) is leaves the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.

title: Which orbital wall is the thickest and strongest?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which orbital wall is the thickest and strongest?
options: Roof (orbital plate of frontal, lesser wing of sphenoid)
Lateral wall (zygomatic and greater wing of sphenoid)
body.explanation: The lateral wall (zygomatic bone + greater wing of the sphenoid) is the strongest. The medial wall, thinned by the lamina papyracea, is the thinnest.

title: What lies in the basilar groove of the pons?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lies in the basilar groove of the pons?
body.explanation: The basilar groove marks the midline of the ventral pons and carries the basilar artery.
option_notes: Lateral.
The basilar artery runs in it.
Lower down.
On the floor of the fourth ventricle.

title: Where do mossy fibres end?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Where do mossy fibres end?
options: On granule cells in the granular layer, in glomeruli
In the molecular layer on basket cells
body.explanation: Mossy fibres synapse with granule cells in glomeruli; granule cells then reach Purkinje cells through parallel fibres.
option_notes: Granule cells in glomeruli.
That is what climbing fibres do.
Not their main ending.
Not their ending.

title: How many bones contribute to the walls of the orbit?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: How many bones contribute to the walls of the orbit?
body.explanation: Frontal, sphenoid and ethmoid (cranial) plus zygomatic, lacrimal, maxilla and palatine (facial): 3 cranial + 4 facial = 7.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the ascending pharyngeal. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which plate develops into the motor neurons?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which plate develops into the motor neurons?
options: The floor plate of the tube
body.explanation: The mantle layer splits into the dorsal alar plate (sensory) and the ventral basal plate (motor), separated by the sulcus limitans, with autonomic neurons in the intermediate zone.
option_notes: Alar plate is sensory.
Roof plate is thin.
Basal plate gives motor neurons.
Floor plate is thin.

title: What neurotransmitter do subthalamic nucleus neurons use?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What neurotransmitter do subthalamic nucleus neurons use?
body.explanation: The subthalamic nucleus has glutamatergic neurons projecting to the internal globus pallidus, whose GABAergic neurons inhibit the thalamus and so inhibit movement.
option_notes: Most basal ganglia outputs use GABA, but not the STN.
Nigra.
The subthalamic nucleus is excitatory, using glutamate.
No.

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Tympanic membrane: the eardrum, closing the inner end of the external auditory canal.
option_notes: Malleus is the outer ossicle, its handle attached to the eardrum.
Stapes is the smallest ossicle, its footplate in the oval window.
Cochlea is the snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear.
The eardrum, closing the inner end of the external auditory canal.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the pons. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the nerve rootlets between pyramid and olive.
This is at the arrow: the bulging middle part of the brainstem.
Not at the arrow; this is the nerves at the angle between pons, medulla and cerebellum.
Not at the arrow; this is the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the cord.

title: What lies medial to the pulvinar?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What lies medial to the pulvinar?
options: The pineal gland and the corpora quadrigemina
body.explanation: The pulvinar lies lateral to the pineal gland, habenula, posterior commissure, quadrigeminal bodies and splenium.
option_notes: These lie medial to the pulvinar.
The internal capsule is lateral to the thalamus.
The lentiform nucleus is lateral to the internal capsule.
The chiasm is far in front.

title: What is the shape of the nasal cavity?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the shape of the nasal cavity?
options: A sphere with a single opening
A flat sheet between the orbits
A cone with its base at the roof
body.explanation: The nasal cavities are the uppermost parts of the respiratory tract and contain the olfactory receptors. They are elongated wedge-shaped spaces with a large inferior base and a narrow superior apex.

title: Through what do olfactory axons pass?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Through what do olfactory axons pass?
body.explanation: Olfactory axons from the olfactory epithelium pass through the cribriform plate and synapse in the olfactory bulbs.

title: Which functional division plans and times skilled voluntary movements?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functional division plans and times skilled voluntary movements?
body.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum, the largest division, takes cortical input via the pontine nuclei and plans, starts and times skilled movements.
option_notes: The lateral hemispheres plan skilled movements.
That serves balance and eye movements.
That regulates tone and posture.
That is the vestibulocerebellum.

title: Which artery gives the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery gives the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)?
body.explanation: SCA and AICA come from the basilar artery; PICA comes from the vertebral artery.
option_notes: PICA is a vertebral branch.
The basilar gives SCA and AICA.
Anterior circulation.
The PCA is a basilar end branch.

title: Name the three subdivisions of the pharynx.
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Name the three subdivisions of the pharynx.
body.explanation: From above downwards: the nasopharynx behind the nose, the oropharynx behind the oral cavity and the laryngopharynx behind the larynx.

title: Which part of the ethmoid forms the upper part of the bony nasal septum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the ethmoid forms the upper part of the bony nasal septum?
body.explanation: The perpendicular plate hangs down from the cribriform plate and, with the vomer, forms the bony nasal septum. The crista galli is its upward projection, anchoring the falx cerebri.

title: What divides the medial wall into two levels?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What divides the medial wall into two levels?
body.explanation: The medial (labyrinthine) wall is divided by the prominence of the facial canal: above it the lateral semicircular canal; below it the promontory, oval window and round window.
option_notes: The facial canal bulge separates upper and lower levels.
The promontory is on the lower level.
The oval window is on the lower level.
The tegmen is the roof.

title: Which deep nucleus is located most laterally?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which deep nucleus is located most laterally?
body.explanation: From lateral to medial: dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial.
option_notes: The dentate is the most lateral.
The fastigial is the most medial.
The globose lies medial to the emboliform.
The emboliform lies medial to the dentate.

title: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres that start salivation?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres that start salivation?
body.explanation: III, VII and IX contact autonomic ganglia: III for pupillary constriction, VII and IX for salivation. X targets thoracic and upper abdominal ganglia.

title: Which functions belong to the thalamus?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which functions belong to the thalamus?
body.explanation: The thalamus maintains consciousness and sleep, filters sensory information for the cortex, and modulates motor responses via the basal ganglia.
option_notes: It takes part in consciousness and sleep.
It filters sensory input.
That is the pineal.
That is the choroid plexus.

title: What is the narrowest part of the facial canal?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What is the narrowest part of the facial canal?
body.explanation: Three segments in the temporal bone: labyrinthine (narrowest, to the geniculate ganglion), tympanic (above the oval window) and mastoid (giving the nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani).

title: Over which days does the neural tube close?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Over which days does the neural tube close?
body.explanation: Neurulation: closure of the neural tube between days 18 and 28.
option_notes: Days 18 to 28.
Too early.
Too late.
Too late.

title: Which three structures form the nasal septum?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which three structures form the nasal septum?
options: Nasal bones, vomer and cribriform plate
body.explanation: The medial wall is the nasal septum, an osteo-cartilaginous structure: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, the vomer bone and the septal cartilage.

title: The lingual artery is divided into three parts by which muscle?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The lingual artery is divided into three parts by which muscle?
body.explanation: The lingual artery arises opposite the tip of the greater cornu of the hyoid, between the superior thyroid and facial arteries, and is divided into three parts by the hyoglossus muscle.

title: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which gyrus or area is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Angular gyrus: the parietal gyrus arching around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.
option_notes: Temporal pole is the front tip of the temporal lobe.
The parietal gyrus arching around the end of the superior temporal sulcus.
Superior temporal gyrus is the top gyrus of the temporal lobe, under the lateral sulcus; its back part holds Wernicke's area.
Cingulate gyrus is the gyrus arching around the corpus callosum on the medial surface (limbic lobe).

title: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Thyroid gland: the butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the trachea, two lobes joined by an isthmus.
option_notes: Cricoid cartilage is the only complete cartilage ring, below the thyroid cartilage.
Hyoid bone is the U-shaped bone above the larynx.
The butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the trachea, two lobes joined by an isthmus.
Trachea is the tube of C-shaped cartilage rings below the cricoid.

title: What does the diencephalon give rise to?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the diencephalon give rise to?
body.explanation: The diencephalon becomes the thalamus, hypothalamus and epithalamus, around the third ventricle.
option_notes: Diencephalic derivatives.
From the telencephalon.
From the metencephalon.
From the myelencephalon.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the skin. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: What does the medial longitudinal fasciculus do?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What does the medial longitudinal fasciculus do?
options: It coordinates conjugate movement of the eyes
It carries the afferent limb of the light reflex
It relays visual information to the cortex
body.explanation: The MLF links CN III, IV, VI and the vestibular system, so the eyes move together in a conjugate way and can compensate for head rotation.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the middle concha. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.

title: Which element is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which element is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to: Magendie and Luschka. The median aperture (Magendie, to the cisterna magna) and two lateral apertures (Luschka, to the cerebellopontine cisterns).
option_notes: This is at the arrow: the outlets of the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow midline cavity between the two thalami.
Not at the arrow; this is the vascular tufts in the ventricles that make CSF.
Not at the arrow; this is the narrow channel through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle.

title: CSF is absorbed mainly through:
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: CSF is absorbed mainly through:
body.explanation: Into the dural venous sinuses, mainly the superior sagittal sinus.
option_notes: It produces CSF.
Not absorption.
Not absorption.
Arachnoid villi and granulations into the sinuses.

title: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which part of the ventricular system is highlighted in orange?
body.explanation: Choroid plexus: the vascular tufts in the ventricles that produce CSF.
option_notes: The vascular tufts in the ventricles that produce CSF.
Lateral ventricle is the C-shaped ventricle in each hemisphere.
Third ventricle is the narrow midline ventricle between the two thalami.
Fourth ventricle is the ventricle between the brainstem and cerebellum.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the epiglottis. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the large shield-shaped cartilage of the larynx (Adam's apple).
Not at the arrow; this is the U-shaped bone above the larynx.
This is at the arrow: the leaf-shaped cartilage behind the tongue base.
Not at the arrow; this is the sheet joining the hyoid to the thyroid cartilage.

title: Which structure is at the arrow?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure is at the arrow?
body.explanation: The arrow points to the temporal lobe. The fully labelled diagram is on the Visual tab.
option_notes: Not at the arrow; this is the gyrus behind the central sulcus.
Not at the arrow; this is the deep groove separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
Not at the arrow; this is the groove between frontal and parietal lobes.
This is at the arrow: the lobe below the lateral sulcus.

title: Which structure separates the coronoid and condylar processes of the mandible?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which structure separates the coronoid and condylar processes of the mandible?
body.explanation: The mandibular notch is the deep concavity between the coronoid process in front and the condylar process behind.

title: Which artery supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: Which artery supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall?
body.explanation: Anterosuperior quadrant: anterior ethmoidal artery. Anteroinferior: branches of the facial and greater palatine arteries. Posterosuperior: sphenopalatine artery. Posteroinferior: branches of the greater palatine artery, which pierces the perpendicular plate of the palatine.

title: What are the nares and the choanae?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: What are the nares and the choanae?
options: The nares open into the pharynx; the choanae onto the face
Nares outside, choanae to the nasopharynx
Both are openings of the maxillary sinus
Both are parts of the nasal septum
body.explanation: The skeletal framework consists mainly of bone and cartilage. Nares: the external opening of the nose. Choanae: open into the nasopharynx.

title: The floor of the orbit is also the roof of which air space?
subject: subj:anat3

body.stem: The floor of the orbit is also the roof of which air space?
